name: Stone
fact: Rock, unweathered. Everything solid you will build starts here.

name: Water
fact: The only common substance found on Earth as solid, liquid and gas.

name: Sun
fact: Every calorie in this game traces back to eight minutes of sunlight.

name: Seed
fact: A plant embryo with a packed lunch, waiting for water.

name: Soil
fact: Broken rock plus dead life. It takes a century to build a centimetre.

name: Sand
fact: Rock ground to between 0.06 and 2 mm, mostly stubborn quartz.

name: Mud
fact: Soil with enough water to lose its grip on itself.

name: Clay
fact: Mineral sheets so fine they slide — the reason clay can be shaped.

name: Adobe
fact: Mud and straw. Half the world's oldest surviving buildings.

name: Brick
fact: Sun-dried mud, standardised. The first mass-produced object.

name: Pot
fact: Fired clay. Once you can boil things, your diet changes forever.

name: Glass
fact: An amorphous solid — no crystal structure. It does not flow, whatever you have heard.

name: Sea
fact: 3.5% salt, and the destination of every mineral rivers carry.

name: Salt
fact: The only rock humans eat. Wars have been fought over it.

name: Brine
fact: Salt water strong enough to dehydrate any microbe that enters it.

name: Ice
fact: Less dense than the water it came from, which is why lakes have fish.

name: Steam
fact: Water carrying five times the energy it needed just to reach boiling.

name: Spark
fact: A fragment of stone, briefly glowing. The start of everything.

name: Flint
fact: Breaks in conchoidal curves, so every fracture leaves an edge. Unlocks Cut.

name: Fire
fact: Carbon meeting oxygen fast enough to glow. Unlocks Heat.

name: Wood
fact: Cellulose in lignin — a natural fibreglass, and a fuel.

name: Charcoal
fact: Wood with everything but the carbon baked out. Burns far hotter.

name: Ash
fact: The minerals a tree pulled from the soil, handed back.

name: Lye
fact: Ash water. Caustic enough to dissolve fat, hair and skin.

name: Soap
fact: One end of the molecule grips grease, the other grips water.

name: Tree
fact: A plant that spends a fortune on a trunk to outgrow its neighbours.

name: Acacia
fact: A savanna thorn tree armed with paired spines — one long and straight, one short and curved.

name: Straw
fact: The stalk left after the grain is taken. Tinder, thatch and bedding.

name: Sprout
fact: A seed that has committed. There is no going back into the shell.

name: Seedling
fact: Roots first, leaves second. Plumbing before solar panels.

name: Plant
fact: A machine that turns light and air into sugar, and asks for nothing.

name: Grass
fact: Grows from the base, so grazing cannot kill it. Covers around 40% of the land.

name: Flower
fact: An advertisement paid for in sugar, aimed at insects.

name: Leaf
fact: A solar panel that must open its pores to breathe, and lose water doing it.

name: Root
fact: Trades sugar with underground fungi for minerals it cannot reach.

name: Bulb
fact: A whole next-season plant, packed in fat leaves, buried for safety.

name: Vine
fact: Skips the cost of a trunk by climbing someone else's.

name: Herb
fact: Leaves whose chemical defences we happen to find delicious.

name: Tea
fact: Green, oolong and black are one plant. Only the oxidation differs.

name: Brewed Tea
fact: Second most consumed drink on Earth, after water itself.

name: Meadow
fact: Not scenery — the density of bloom that makes a pollinator colony viable.

name: Nectar
fact: Roughly 25% sugar, made deliberately and given away on purpose.

name: Bee
fact: Forages 5 km out and reports good ground back to the hive by dancing.

name: Honey
fact: Under 18% water. Nothing can grow in it, so it never spoils.

name: Beeswax
fact: Costs the hive 8 g of honey for every 1 g secreted.

name: Candle
fact: The wick does not burn. It pumps liquid wax up into the flame.

name: Fruit
fact: A bribe wrapped around a seed, aimed at anything that travels.

name: Yeast
fact: A single-celled fungus living on fruit skins. Unlocks Ferment.

name: Chilli
fact: Capsaicin repels mammals and does nothing at all to birds.

name: Grape
fact: Picked near 24% sugar — exactly what yeast needs to reach 13% alcohol.

name: Cucumber
fact: About 95% water, held up entirely by cell wall pressure.

name: Tomato
fact: A berry, and unusually full of glutamate — which is why it reads as savoury.

name: Apple
fact: Seeds never breed true. Every named variety is a clone of one lucky tree.

name: Olive
fact: Inedibly bitter raw. Every olive you have eaten was cured first.

name: Wheat
fact: Bred for 10,000 years above all to stop dropping its own seed.

name: Rice
fact: Tolerates flooding, so the water itself does the weeding.

name: Sugarcane
fact: A giant grass that stores sugar in the stalk instead of the seed.

name: Potato
fact: Not a root — a swollen underground stem. That is why it has eyes.

name: Onion
fact: Cut it and two chemicals that were kept apart meet, and you cry.

name: Garlic
fact: Whole, it barely smells. The smell is a wound response.

name: Cabbage
fact: Same species as kale, broccoli, sprouts and cauliflower. All of them.

name: Field
fact: One plant, no competitors — the most productive and most fragile system in farming.

name: Harvest
fact: The narrow window the entire calendar of settled life is built around.

name: Grain
fact: A seed we eat before it ever gets to be a plant.

name: Flour
fact: Ground grain. Porridge came 30,000 years before anyone baked it.

name: Malt
fact: Barley sprouted then killed, its starch already turned to sugar.

name: Dough
fact: Wet, worked flour: an elastic protein net strong enough to hold gas.

name: Pasta Dough
fact: Egg instead of yeast. The protein sets the shape on cooking.

name: Pastry
fact: Layers of flour separated by cold butter, waiting for steam.

name: Cake Batter
fact: Sugar steals water from the flour, which is what keeps cake tender.

name: Risen Dough
fact: Full of carbon dioxide the yeast exhaled and the gluten refused to let go.

name: Sourdough Starter
fact: Wild yeast and lactobacilli, kept alive by daily feeding. Livestock, really.

name: Flatbread
fact: The oldest bread. Steam alone puffs it, in under two minutes.

name: Bread
fact: A foam of carbon dioxide, set solid by heat.

name: Sourdough
fact: Slower, sourer, and it keeps for days because the acid holds mould off.

name: Noodle
fact: The oldest found are 4,000-year-old millet noodles from Lajia, China.

name: Pasta
fact: Al dente is the few seconds between the starch swelling and the protein firming.

name: Cake
fact: Set the scaffold before the air escapes, or it falls.

name: Wort
fact: Sweet barley water. Boiling it sterilised beer centuries before germ theory.

name: Beer
fact: Boiled, and therefore safe. Older than writing, possibly older than bread.

name: Grape Juice
fact: Crushing brings the wild yeast on the skin to the sugar inside.

name: Wine
fact: Stops near 15% — the point where yeast is killed by its own waste.

name: Vinegar
fact: Literally 'sour wine'. A second fermentation, by a different organism.

name: Apple Juice
fact: Browns within minutes — the same enzyme reaction as a bruise.

name: Cider
fact: Apples carry their own yeast and sugar. Left alone, juice becomes cider.

name: Olive Oil
fact: Squeezed from fruit flesh. Cold press means pressure and nothing else.

name: Cane Juice
fact: Must be crushed within a day, before the cane eats its own sugar.

name: Sugar
fact: One of the purest substances in any kitchen — near 100% sucrose.

name: Caramel
fact: Hundreds of new compounds, none of which were in the sugar.

name: Mead Must
fact: Honey watered down until life can live in it again.

name: Mead
fact: Honey, water and time. No field and no harvest required.

name: Sauerkraut
fact: The bacteria that sour it were already living on the cabbage.

name: Kimchi
fact: The same lactic fermentation as sauerkraut, run cold and spiced.

name: Pickle
fact: A brined pickle is alive and souring. A vinegar one arrives sour.

name: Passata
fact: Cooked tomato gives up far more lycopene than raw. Some food is better cooked.

name: Herb Oil
fact: Aroma compounds dissolve in fat, not water. Oil is the better solvent.

name: Pasture
fact: Humans cannot digest grass. Grazers are the machine that converts it.

name: Aurochs
fact: 1.8 m at the shoulder, foul-tempered, extinct since 1627.

name: Cow
fact: Every cow alive descends from roughly 80 tamed aurochs.

name: Milk
fact: Around 90 kg of grass a day becomes some 28 litres — and only after a calf.

name: Chicken
fact: Domesticated jungle bird. Around three alive per living human.

name: Egg
fact: A chalk shell with seven to seventeen thousand pores, because the embryo breathes.

name: Fish
fact: The first vertebrates. Your skeleton is a variation on their design.

name: Lizard
fact: Over 7,000 species, and every one an ectotherm — basking in the sun is a requirement, not a habit.

name: Snake
fact: Legless, with 175 to 400-plus vertebrae — and, in most species, only one working lung.

name: Turtle
fact: A shell of 50 to 60 of its own bones — ribs and vertebrae, fused outward and capped in keratin.

name: Rattlesnake
fact: Its rattle is hollow keratin segments — modified tail scales, buzzed by a dedicated muscle.

name: Salt Fish
fact: Fed medieval Europe through winter and crossed oceans without ice.

name: Meat
fact: Tenderness depends almost entirely on how hard that muscle worked.

name: Mince
fact: Cutting across the fibres is why a burger beats the same cut whole.

name: Roast
fact: The Maillard reaction: hundreds of aromas that did not exist raw.

name: Cured Meat
fact: Salt does not kill the microbes. It leaves them nothing to drink.

name: Bacon
fact: Wood smoke is genuinely antimicrobial. The flavour was a side effect.

name: Sausage
fact: A way to make offcuts keep, and travel.

name: Meatball
fact: Egg binds it. Without a binder, mince squeezes out its own juice.

name: Broth
fact: Tough collagen dissolved into gelatin. Cheap cuts make the best.

name: Aspic
fact: Proof in a bowl that the collagen really did dissolve.

name: Soup
fact: Almost every cuisine on Earth begins one the same way: onion, slowly.

name: Cream
fact: Fat floats. Cream is milk that has been left alone.

name: Butter
fact: Fat globules battered until they break and stick to each other.

name: Ghee
fact: Water gone, solids strained. Keeps for months without a fridge.

name: Yoghurt
fact: The bacteria eat the lactose, which is why the intolerant can eat it.

name: Curd
fact: Acid makes casein clump. The fastest cheese there is.

name: Cheese
fact: Salted curd. From here, the only ingredient left is time.

name: Aged Cheese
fact: Those crunchy crystals in old parmesan are free amino acids.

name: Mould
fact: Its spores are in every room you have ever stood in.

name: Blue Cheese
fact: Skewered with holes, because the mould needs air to grow inward.

name: Penicillin
fact: An accident on a windowsill in 1928, and a decade of work to make it a drug.

name: Ice Cream
fact: Stirring while freezing keeps the crystals microscopic. That is the trick.

name: Mayonnaise
fact: Lecithin holds oil inside water that would rather not hold it.

name: Boiled Egg
fact: White sets at 63 °C, yolk at 70 °C. Everything happens in between.

name: Cooked Rice
fact: Raw starch is nearly indigestible. Cooked, it feeds most of the world.

name: Sushi Rice
fact: Sushi began as preservation — fish kept safe in souring rice.

name: Baked Potato
fact: Dry heat makes it floury. The same potato boiled stays waxy.

name: Chips
fact: Escaping steam is what keeps the oil out. Cool oil means greasy chips.

name: Salad
fact: Salt early and osmosis empties every cell. Dress it at the table.

name: Greek Salad
fact: No lettuce in a real one. Just what ripens together, in the same soil.

name: Cheese Toastie
fact: Young cheese flows; very old cheese has no water left and splits.

name: Pizza Base
fact: A Neapolitan oven runs at 450 °C and is done in 90 seconds.

name: Pizza
fact: Tomato on flatbread is far older than the flag story, and belonged to the poor.

name: Apple Pie
fact: Pectin glues apple cells together and survives the oven.

name: Grilled Fish
fact: Sets at 50 °C. Fish never had to hold itself up against gravity.

name: Dinner
fact: Stone, water, sun and a seed. All of agriculture, on one plate.

name: Feast
fact: Nutritionally unnecessary. Every human society does it anyway.

name: Philosopher's Stone
fact: Never found. Chemistry was the consolation prize.

name: Stone Soup
fact: A fable about how to get a village to feed itself.

name: Gingerbread Man
fact: Elizabeth I had them baked in the likeness of visiting dignitaries.

name: Corn Dolly
fact: The last sheaf, woven into a figure to hold the harvest spirit.

name: Scarecrow
fact: Crows learn its face in two days. It works on everything else.

name: Cornucopia
fact: The broken horn of the goat that nursed Zeus. It refilled forever.

name: Ambrosia
fact: Food of the gods, said to confer immortality on anyone who ate it.

name: Manna
fact: Appeared each dawn, rotted by dusk. Nobody agrees what it was.

name: Golden Egg
fact: A story about not understanding the system you live off.

name: Sickle
fact: A curved flint blade. The tool that turned a field into a harvest.

name: Granary
fact: Surplus, stored. It bought the first bad year, and the first bureaucracy.

name: Smoked Fish
fact: Preserved by phenols before it is ever properly cooked.

name: Greenhouse
fact: Holds heat by stopping warm air rising away, not by trapping infrared.

name: Early Crop
fact: Borrowed warmth, and a harvest weeks ahead of the weather.

name: Barrel
fact: Oak bent by steam. Storage that flavours what it stores.

name: Aged Wine
fact: Oxygen through the staves, vanillin out of the oak.

name: Clean Hands
fact: The cheapest public health intervention ever discovered.

name: Garlic Butter
fact: Fat as a delivery system for a plant’s wound chemistry.

name: Garlic Bread
fact: Bread is porous enough to drink fat. That is the whole idea.

name: Wrap
fact: Flatbread used as cutlery, which is how most of the world ate.

name: Spaghetti & Meatballs
fact: Invented in New York, where meat was suddenly cheap.

name: Malt Vinegar
fact: Beer that met the wrong bacteria, to everyone’s benefit.

name: Caramel Sauce
fact: Fat and water blocking sugar from crystallising again.

name: Sundae
fact: Your tongue reads the contrast, not the average.

name: Choucroute
fact: Two autumn preservations, eaten together in midwinter.

name: Breakfast
fact: A 1920s public relations campaign that never wore off.

name: Cheeseboard
fact: Acid and sugar, cutting fat. Mechanics dressed as tradition.

name: Tzatziki
fact: Yoghurt with the whey drained out, and the protein left behind.

name: Potato Salad
fact: Dress it warm. Cold starch will not drink anything.

name: Egg Sandwich
fact: Named after a man who would not leave the card table.

name: Fish & Chips
fact: Britain’s national dish, assembled entirely from imports.

name: Pilaf
fact: Fat around every grain, so the starch never glues them together.

name: Salted Dough
fact: Salt does not just season bread — it tightens the gluten and slows the yeast.

name: Creamed Butter
fact: Butter and sugar beaten pale. The air whipped in is the leavening.

name: Cake Mix
fact: Fat, sugar and egg, emulsified — before any flour goes near it.

name: Sweet Cream
fact: Sugar lowers the freezing point, which is what keeps ice cream scoopable.

name: Breadcrumb
fact: Stale bread, crushed. It holds moisture that would otherwise be squeezed out.

name: Meatball Mix
fact: Mince and crumb, waiting for a binder.

name: Meatballs in Sauce
fact: Simmered in tomato, which cooks them through and seasons the sauce back.

name: Garlic Yoghurt
fact: Raw garlic stirred through yoghurt, which tames it without cooking it.

name: Olive Salad
fact: Tomato, cucumber and olive — everything that ripens in the same month.

name: Batter
fact: Flour and beer. The bubbles make it light; the alcohol boils off fast and crisps it.

name: Battered Fish
fact: A raw coat of batter, sealing the fish before it ever meets the oil.

name: Fried Fish
fact: The batter sets into a shell and the fish inside steams in its own moisture.

name: Rubbed Flour
fact: Butter worked into flour until it looks like breadcrumbs. Water comes last.

name: Salted Mince
fact: Salt draws out protein that makes the mince sticky enough to hold together.

name: Egg Mayonnaise
fact: Chopped egg bound in its own emulsion — yolk meeting yolk.

name: Kimchi Paste
fact: Chilli and garlic, the flavour engine of the ferment.

name: Salted Cabbage
fact: Brined until limp, so the paste can reach every leaf.

name: Tempered Clay
fact: Clay cut with sand so it can dry and fire without cracking.

name: Stoneware
fact: Fired hard enough to hold liquid without a glaze.

name: Limestone
fact: Compacted seabed — shells and skeletons, pressed for aeons.

name: Cement Meal
fact: Ground limestone and clay, waiting for the kiln.

name: Cement
fact: The glue. Roughly a tenth of humanity's carbon dioxide.

name: Mortar
fact: Cement paste with sand in it to stop it shrinking.

name: Concrete
fact: Rock, glued. The most used material on Earth after water.

name: River
fact: Fresh to taste, but never pure — every river carries dissolved rock to the sea.

name: Goat
fact: Domesticated from wild bezoars; browses scrub and rock where cattle starve.

name: Carbon
fact: Four bonds in every direction. Every molecule life is built from hangs off it.

name: Oxygen
fact: Most of your mass by atom count. Almost never found alone either — it pairs up on contact.

name: Hydrogen
fact: The first element, made in the first minutes of the universe. Almost never found alone.

name: Nitrogen
fact: Two atoms locked by the strongest bond there is, N2 — four fifths of the air.

name: Sulfur
fact: Yellow, volcanic, and the reason two amino acids can staple themselves together.

name: Phosphorus
fact: Carries the energy and holds DNA together. The scarcest of the six.

name: Legume
fact: A plant that hosts bacteria in its roots and pays them in sugar.

name: Bone
fact: Collagen for spring, calcium phosphate for stiffness. Neither works alone.

name: Shell
fact: Calcium carbonate, laid down by a fringe of tissue called the mantle.

name: Carbon Dioxide
fact: What burning makes and what leaves eat.

name: Glucose
fact: What photosynthesis actually produces. Everything else is built from it.

name: Starch
fact: Thousands of glucose units chained for storage.

name: Amino Acid
fact: Twenty of them, in every living thing, all the same handedness.

name: Cysteine
fact: The amino acid carrying sulfur. It can bond to another of its own kind.

name: Dipeptide
fact: Two amino acids joined, and one water molecule gone.

name: Polypeptide
fact: A chain in a specific order, written in DNA and read by a ribosome.

name: Protein
fact: A chain folded into one shape. The shape is the function.

name: Disulfide Bond
fact: Two cysteines, cross-linked. What makes hair hair.

name: Keratin
fact: Hair, nail, horn and hoof — all the same protein, differently packed.

name: Denatured Protein
fact: Unfolded, tangled, set. This is what cooking is.

name: ATP
fact: The cell spends its own body weight in this every day.

name: Nucleotide
fact: Sugar, phosphate and a base. Four of them spell everything alive.

name: DNA
fact: The instructions, in four letters, for building the thing holding it.

name: Membrane
fact: Two layers of fat, tails inward. Life needs an inside.

name: Cell
fact: The smallest thing that is unambiguously alive.

name: Tissue
fact: Cells of one kind, doing one job together.

name: Muscle
fact: Protein filaments ratcheting past each other.

name: Collagen
fact: A third of all the protein in you, wound in triple helices.

name: Gelatin
fact: Collagen unwound by heat, and it sets as it cools.

name: Enzyme
fact: A protein with a pocket shaped to hold one particular molecule.

name: Alpha Helix
fact: A chain coiled into a spring, held by hydrogen bonds four residues apart.

name: Beta Sheet
fact: Chains lying side by side, pleated like a folded fan. Silk is almost nothing else.

name: Ribosome
fact: Two thirds RNA — and the RNA, not the protein, is the part that does the chemistry.

name: Messenger RNA
fact: A working copy of one gene. Short-lived on purpose, so the cell can stop just by letting it decay.

name: Resistance
fact: The survivors of a course of antibiotics are, by definition, the ones it did not kill.

name: Hydrogen Gas
fact: Two hydrogen atoms, bonded — H2. This is the form that actually exists in a jar.

name: Oxygen Gas
fact: Two oxygen atoms, double-bonded — O2. The gas in every breath you take.

name: Ore
fact: Rock with enough of a useful mineral in it to be worth digging up — usually a metal.

name: Cinnabar
fact: Bright red mercury sulfide, and mercury's one and only important ore.

name: Rutile
fact: Titanium dioxide, and — along with ilmenite — the only titanium ore that's ever been worth mining.

name: Iron
fact: Iron ore needs a furnace hot enough to reach 1,500°C to give up its metal.

name: Copper
fact: One of the few metals nature hands you pure — the first one anyone learned to smelt, around 5000 BC.

name: Gold
fact: Chemically inert enough that it is still found lying around as pure metal — no smelting required.

name: Silver
fact: For most of history this did not come from silver ore at all — it came out of lead.

name: Tin
fact: Melts at just 232°C — one of the easiest metals there is to work.

name: Lead
fact: So easy to coax out of its ore that people in the Near East were using it before recorded history began.

name: Zinc
fact: Boils at 907°C — cooler than it takes to smelt its own ore, so the metal evaporates unless you catch it.

name: Mercury
fact: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature — freed from its ore just by roasting it.

name: Aluminium
fact: The commonest metal in Earth's crust — once so hard to isolate it cost more than gold, until 1886.

name: Nickel
fact: Named after a mischievous spirit — miners dug up a copper-look ore and got no copper out of it.

name: Chromium
fact: Pulled from its ore by a reaction hot enough to run on its own once lit — burning aluminium for the oxygen.

name: Titanium
fact: So reactive that heating its ore with carbon — the trick that works for iron — just makes a ceramic instead.

name: Platinum
fact: Melts at 1,768°C — so hot the first people to work it never melted it, just sintered the grains with gold.

name: Uranium
fact: Named for a planet, and it took fifty years between finding the ore and finally isolating the metal itself.

name: Helium
fact: First spotted in sunlight during an 1868 eclipse, not found on Earth for another 27 years.

name: Neon
fact: Trace enough in air — 18 parts per million — that it took liquefying the whole atmosphere to find it.

name: Magnesium
fact: The third most abundant element dissolved in seawater — and it burns at about 3,100°C.

name: Calcium
fact: The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust, and the third most abundant metal.

name: Sodium
fact: A metal that catches fire on contact with water — which is why it is never found free in nature.

name: Potassium
fact: Reacts with water hard enough to ignite its own hydrogen, burning with a lilac flame.

name: Yellowcake
fact: Powdered uranium concentrate — not the metal yet, just the ore boiled down to something worth shipping.

name: Flax
fact: Humans were using wild flax for textiles 30,000 years ago, long before farming it.

name: Fibre
fact: What is left of a flax stalk after the soft inner parts have rotted away.

name: Thread
fact: The oldest known twisted fibre is around 50,000 to 40,000 BC — older than farming, pottery or metal.

name: Cloth
fact: Two sets of thread interlaced at right angles: warp one way, weft the other.

name: Clothing
fact: Cloth cut and stitched to the shape of a body — the point of the whole fibre chain.

name: Pulp
fact: Cellulose fibre beaten loose and suspended in water, waiting to be drained into a sheet.

name: Paper
fact: A thin sheet of matted cellulose fibres. The pulp process is credited to Cai Lun, a Han court eunuch.

name: Oak Gall
fact: A wasp lays an egg in an oak bud and the tree grows a hard apple-like ball around the larva.

name: Ink
fact: Iron gall ink was Europe's standard ink for the 1,400 years between the 5th and 19th centuries.

name: Mirror
fact: Silver deposited on the back of a sheet of glass — Justus von Liebig's process, 1835.

name: Enriched Uranium
fact: Natural uranium is over 99% U-238. Weapons grade means 85% or more of the rarer U-235.

name: Nuclear Warhead
fact: Critical mass is the least fissile material that will sustain a chain reaction. Past it, the rate only climbs.

name: Book
fact: A stack of pages bound at one edge — the biggest advance in bookmaking before the printing press.

name: Pig
fact: Domesticated twice over, independently: near the Tigris, and separately in China.

name: Lard
fact: A semi-solid white fat, rendered straight out of a pig by steam, boiling or dry heat.

name: Sheep
fact: Grazes grass flat where a goat would rather climb and browse the scrub instead.

name: Wool
fact: Not just hair — the crimp and the microscopic scale are what let it felt and spin.

name: Horse
fact: Its teeth never stop erupting, worn down by a lifetime of grazing.

name: Duck
fact: Almost every domestic duck breed on Earth comes down from one wild bird: the mallard.

name: Turkey
fact: Spends all day foraging the ground, then flies up into a tree every night to roost.

name: Wolf
fact: Dogs and wolves share a common wolf ancestor — today's wolves are cousins, not quite the parents.

name: Deer
fact: Lives in the seam between forest and open ground — cover on one side, grazing on the other.

name: Brown Bear
fact: Along parts of the Alaskan coast, this bear eats almost nothing but salmon while the run lasts.

name: Kangaroo
fact: Hop it fast enough and it costs less energy, not more — the opposite of most ways of moving.

name: Koala
fact: Eats almost nothing but eucalyptus — and out of 600-plus species on offer, sticks to about 30.

name: Dingo
fact: A domestic dog gone wild — feral for well over 3,000 years, and now Australia's apex predator.

name: Platypus
fact: A mammal that lays eggs, carries a venomous spur, and hunts by sensing electricity.

name: Elephant
fact: Pushes over trees for a living, and does it thoroughly enough to turn woodland into grassland.

name: Lion
fact: The most social cat there is — it lives in family groups where other big cats hunt alone.

name: Zebra
fact: Those stripes are there to stop flies landing, not to help it hide or keep cool.

name: Giraffe
fact: A heart that runs at roughly twice human blood pressure, just to get blood up to the brain.

name: Dromedary Camel
fact: The hump is fat, not water — up to 36 kg of it, burned for energy when food runs short.

name: Chromatin
fact: DNA spooled round protein beads. Two metres of it fits in a nucleus six microns across.

name: Chromosome
fact: Chromatin wound down about ten thousand times tighter. Only then can you see one down a microscope.

name: Gene
fact: One stretch that codes for one thing. Barely 2% of your genome is doing that.

name: Nucleus
fact: A double membrane with a few thousand doors in it, keeping the genome apart from the machinery.

name: Microtubule
fact: A hollow tube of two proteins, 25 nm across. It builds the spindle and it drives the sperm's tail.

name: Mitosis
fact: One cell into two identical ones. Nearly every cell you have was made this way.

name: Meiosis
fact: Two divisions, one copy of the DNA. That is how you get half a set instead of a whole one.

name: Sperm
fact: Head five microns wide, tail ten times longer. The testes make 200 to 300 million a day.

name: Ovum
fact: One of the largest cells in your body, and the only one you can see without a microscope.

name: Polar Body
fact: Meiosis in the female divides unfairly on purpose: three cells get chromosomes and almost nothing else.

name: Zygote
fact: One cell, one full set of chromosomes again, and about thirty hours before it divides.

name: Morula
fact: Sixteen cells in a ball. Named after a mulberry, which is the least clinical word in embryology.

name: Blastocyst
fact: A hundred cells around a puddle. The cells pumped in the salt and the water followed.

name: Stem Cell
fact: Undecided. Given the right signal it becomes any of the 200-odd cell types you are built from.

name: Gastrula
fact: Where a ball of cells becomes layers, and the layers decide what everything will be.

name: Embryo
fact: Eight weeks, and every major organ is at least started. None of them work properly yet.

name: Fetus
fact: Latin for offspring. From week nine the organs are all there, unfinished and not all in place.

name: Human
fact: Full term runs 39 to 40 weeks. Then labour ends the pregnancy and a newborn leaves the body it grew inside.

name: Cotton
fact: A fibre that grows in a boll wrapped around the seeds. The plant grew it to help them travel.

name: Maize
fact: Cannot sow itself. The kernels stay stuck to the cob, so without someone to plant it, it ends.

name: Popcorn
fact: Steam at 135 psi bursting the hull, and the starch inside foaming out. Only one kind of maize does it.

name: Barley
fact: Handles salty ground that would finish wheat. Most of the world crop is eaten by animals, not people.

name: Oat
fact: Started life as a weed in other people's wheat fields and got domesticated more or less by accident.

name: Soybean
fact: 36% protein and 20% oil by weight, and it makes its own nitrogen. A crop that asks for very little.

name: Tofu
fact: Cheese, made from a bean. Curdle soy milk with a salt, press the curds, cut into blocks.

name: Pea
fact: A monk grew several thousand of these, counted what came out, and got modern genetics.

name: Carrot
fact: Purple, for most of its history. The orange one is a Dutch invention, and fairly recent at that.

name: Lettuce
fact: 94.9% water, so it cannot be frozen, canned or dried. Eat it now or do not eat it.

name: Pumpkin
fact: A berry. The record one weighed 1,246.9 kg, which is a great deal of berry.

name: Beet
fact: The red pigment goes straight through some people. Pink urine, harmless, and it has a name: beeturia.

name: Lemon
fact: Not a wild species at all — a hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange, two other fruits entirely.

name: Strawberry
fact: Not a berry. Each seed on the outside is an achene — a whole separate fruit with a seed in it.

name: Banana
fact: A berry, growing on the largest herb on Earth. What looks like a trunk is not a trunk.

name: Pear
fact: A pome, like the apple, but picked green and hard on purpose — it finishes ripening off the tree.

name: Cherry
fact: Crack the stone, chew the kernel inside, and it releases hydrogen cyanide. So do not do that.

name: Fig
fact: A fruit with all the flowers folded away inside, and a wasp that crawls in to reach them.

name: Coffee
fact: Not a bean. It is the seed of a fruit called a cherry, and it tastes of nothing until it is roasted.

name: Brewed Coffee
fact: Roasted, ground, steeped in hot water, then filtered back out. That is the entire method.

name: Cocoa
fact: The pods grow straight out of the trunk. Raw, the beans inside are bitter and taste of nothing much.

name: Cocoa Bean
fact: Heaped up for days until the pulp liquefies and ferments. Skip that and it stays harshly bitter.

name: Chocolate
fact: Ground until the particles are under 20 micrometres — finer than the tongue can detect.

name: Glycine
fact: The smallest of the twenty, and the only one with no handedness — its side chain is one hydrogen.

name: Alanine
fact: The next simplest after glycine. Muscle uses it to post spare nitrogen back to the liver.

name: Serine
fact: Named after silk. The nucleophile at the heart of a serine protease is one of these.

name: Proline
fact: Its side chain loops back onto the backbone. That kink is what breaks an alpha helix.

name: Tyrosine
fact: Made from phenylalanine, and turned into dopamine, adrenaline, thyroid hormone and melanin.

name: Aspartic Acid
fact: Half of aspartame. In plants it is the parent of four amino acids you cannot make yourself.

name: Glutamic Acid
fact: Savoury on its own. This is what umami is, and MSG is the salt they sell it as.

name: Glutamine
fact: The most abundant free amino acid in your blood, and how the body moves ammonia around safely.

name: Asparagine
fact: The first amino acid anyone ever isolated, out of asparagus juice, in 1806.

name: Arginine
fact: The only thing your body makes nitric oxide out of, and the last stop before urea.

name: Valine
fact: Swap a glutamate for one of these at position six of beta-globin and you have sickle-cell disease.

name: Leucine
fact: Eat enough of it and muscle starts building protein. It is the signal as well as the material.

name: Isoleucine
fact: One of only two of the twenty with two chiral centres, and it is built out of the other one.

name: Threonine
fact: The last of the twenty to be found, in 1935, and one of only two with two chiral centres.

name: Methionine
fact: AUG codes for this and nothing else, and AUG is where the ribosome starts reading.

name: Lysine
fact: Cereal grains are short of it and pulses are full of it. That is why beans and bread go together.

name: Histidine
fact: Its ring has a pKa near 6, close enough to swap a proton in a living cell. Active sites are full of it.

name: Phenylalanine
fact: The one on the aspartame warning label. People with PKU cannot break it down.

name: Tryptophan
fact: The biggest of the twenty, and the raw material for serotonin, melatonin and vitamin B3.

name: Quicklime
fact: Limestone with the carbon dioxide cooked out of it. Add water and it gets hot enough to boil.

name: Fluorite
fact: Named from *fluere*, to flow — it was a smelting flux long before anyone knew it held an element.

name: Kelp
fact: Not a plant at all. A brown alga that grips rock instead of rooting, and can grow half a metre a day.

name: Borax
fact: Traded down the Silk Road from Tibetan lake beds in the 8th century, long before anyone had heard of boron.

name: Chlorine
fact: Named for its colour — khlōrós, pale green — and the first gas ever used as a weapon, at Ypres in 1915.

name: Fluorine
fact: Reacts with everything but the lightest noble gases. The chemists who chased it are called fluorine martyrs.

name: Bromine
fact: The only nonmetal that is liquid at room temperature. Named brômos, Greek for stench.

name: Iodine
fact: Found by accident in seaweed ash in 1811, and named for the violet vapour that came off it.

name: Silicon
fact: 27.2% of the crust by weight, second only to oxygen — and almost never found loose.

name: Boron
fact: Claimed in 1808 and arguably not made pure until 1909 — a hundred and one years of nearly-boron.

name: Arsenic
fact: Skips the liquid state entirely: heat it and at 614°C it goes straight from solid to gas.

name: Selenium
fact: Named for the moon, because tellurium had already taken the earth. Nearly all of it comes out of copper.

name: Antimony
fact: Egyptians were painting their eyes with its sulfide by about 3100 BC, which is where kohl comes from.

name: Germanium
fact: Mendeleev left a gap for it in 1869 and called it ekasilicon. Winkler found it in a silver ore in 1886.

name: Tellurium
fact: About as rare in the crust as platinum, and a 15 mg dose gives you garlic breath for months.

name: Argon
fact: Third most abundant gas in the air, and nearly every atom of it was once a potassium atom.

name: Krypton
fact: From 1960 to 1983 the metre was defined as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of one krypton-86 line.

name: Pyrolusite
fact: Manganese dioxide — the black that Neanderthals painted caves with, and glassmakers' soap.

name: Molybdenite
fact: Soft, grey, greasy and metallic — for centuries nobody could tell it from graphite or from lead ore.

name: Osmiridium
fact: Hard grains of osmium and iridium, already alloyed, sitting in the river sand with the platinum.

name: Manganese
fact: The reason steel bends instead of cracking — it ties up the sulfur that would split it while hot.

name: Cobalt
fact: Named for a goblin. Miners got no copper out of the blue ore and blamed the kobold — same joke as nickel.

name: Tungsten
fact: Melts at 3,422°C — the highest melting point of any metal, which is why light bulbs used it.

name: Molybdenum
fact: Its name is just the Greek word for lead, because for centuries nobody could tell the two ores apart.

name: Vanadium
fact: Named for a Norse goddess because its compounds are so colourful. Nine tenths of it is scraped out of slag.

name: Cadmium
fact: Boils at 767°C, cooler than zinc does — which is exactly how it gets separated from the zinc it hides in.

name: Palladium
fact: Over half of it is sitting in catalytic converters, turning car exhaust into something less poisonous.

name: Rhodium
fact: Named after a rose, for the colour of one of its salts. Under one part per billion of the crust.

name: Iridium
fact: A thin iridium layer in the clay worldwide is the fingerprint of the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.

name: Osmium
fact: The densest element that occurs in nature — 22.59 g/cm³, about twice the density of lead.

name: Ruthenium
fact: About 100 parts per trillion of the crust, and roughly 30 tonnes a year. Named, in Latin, for Russia.

name: Rhenium
fact: One part per billion of the crust, and no ore of its own — it is always somebody else's by-product.

name: Hafnium
fact: Chemically almost indistinguishable from zirconium, so it hid inside it until 1923 — then it got Copenhagen.

name: Zirconium
fact: Neutrons pass straight through it, which is why nuclear fuel is wrapped in zirconium and not in steel.

name: Tantalum
fact: Named for the man in the myth who stood in water he could never drink, tantalised for eternity.

name: Niobium
fact: Named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, because for decades nobody could tell it from tantalum.

name: Scandium
fact: Mendeleev left a gap in the table and described what belonged there. Ten years later, someone found it.

name: Yttrium
fact: One small Swedish quarry, Ytterby, ended up with four elements named after it. This is the first of them.

name: Pollucite
fact: A zeolite up to a quarter caesium by weight — most of the world's supply sits under one Canadian lake.

name: Monazite
fact: Reddish phosphate sand, heavy enough to survive weathering and pile up on beaches. Full of rare earths.

name: Rare earth
fact: The lanthanides as they actually come: a mixture, and famously hard to separate into its members.

name: Baryte
fact: Barium sulfate, better known as heavy spar. Most of what's mined goes down oil wells as drilling mud.

name: Lithium
fact: The least dense metal there is, and one of only three that float on water — while reacting with it.

name: Caesium
fact: The second is defined as 9,192,631,770 cycles of one caesium transition. This metal is the clock.

name: Rubidium
fact: Named for the deep red lines in its spectrum. Parting it from caesium takes about 30 recrystallisations.

name: Beryllium
fact: Nearly transparent to X-rays, which is why the window on an X-ray tube is very often made of it.

name: Strontium
fact: Named after a Scottish village, and it is what makes the red in fireworks.

name: Barium
fact: You drink it so your gut shows up on an X-ray — safe only because that one barium salt won't dissolve.

name: Radium
fact: Painted onto watch dials to make them glow, by women told to lick their brushes to a point. It killed them.

name: Thorium
fact: Three times as common as uranium, and for a century most of what was mined went into gas lamp mantles.

name: Plutonium
fact: Not mined — made. Uranium-238 in a reactor swallows a neutron and, two beta decays later, is plutonium.

name: Polonium
fact: Marie Curie found it first and named it for Poland. By mass it is 250,000 times more toxic than cyanide.

name: Cerium
fact: As common in the crust as copper, and the one rare earth that will oxidise its own way out of the mix.

name: Lanthanum
fact: Its name means 'to lie hidden' — it was found hiding inside what everyone took for pure cerium.

name: Neodymium
fact: Nd2Fe14B — the strongest permanent magnets known. The name just means 'new twin'.

name: Samarium
fact: The first element ever named after a person — and you get it by boiling it off a bath of lanthanum.

name: Europium
fact: The red on old colour TV screens, and the glow in euro banknotes under UV. Also the softest lanthanide.

name: Gadolinium
fact: Sticks to a magnet only below 20°C, and swallows neutrons better than any other stable nuclide.

name: Promethium
fact: No stable isotope at all. About 560 grams exist in the entire crust, made by uranium quietly fissioning.

name: Krypton–Xenon Mix
fact: What an air plant actually gives you: the two rarest stable gases, still mixed together.

name: Xenon
fact: In 1962 it formed a compound, and "the noble gases do not react" quietly stopped being true.

name: Bismuth
fact: Decays with a half-life a billion times the age of the universe, so everyone just calls it stable.

name: Smoke
fact: An aerosol of soot, condensed tar and ash — the part of the fuel that never finished burning.

name: Forge
fact: A hearth with a pipe into the fire. More air means a faster burn, and a faster burn means more heat.

name: Stockfish
fact: Unsalted cod dried on open racks by cold wind. Loses about 80% of its water and keeps for years.

name: Bottle
fact: A bubble of glass inflated down a hollow pipe, then worked into a shape.

name: Bone Char
fact: Charred bone, porous and black. The standard decolouriser in cane-sugar refining.

name: Blackware
fact: Fired black, because the starved fire took its oxygen from the iron in the clay.

name: Air
fact: 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon — and the whole of it weighs about 5.15 × 10^18 kg.

name: Sky
fact: Not a thing — a colour. Sunlight scattered by air molecules, blue scattered hardest.

name: Wind
fact: Air levelling out a pressure difference the sun made by heating one place more.

name: Dust
fact: Silt held up by air. Dry ground puts thousands of millions of tonnes up a year.

name: Cloud
fact: Droplets condensed onto specks a hundredth their size, about 0.2 micrometres across.

name: Mist
fact: The same droplets as fog, thinner. The only line between them is whether you can still see a kilometre.

name: Fog
fact: A stratus cloud that reached the ground. It loses its Latin name the moment it touches.

name: Dew
fact: Water that condensed onto something cold, not water that fell. It starts at the dew point.

name: Frost
fact: Not frozen dew. Water vapour deposits straight onto a cold surface as ice, skipping liquid altogether.

name: Rain
fact: Drops from 0.1 to 9 mm across, flattened rather than tear-shaped, and breaking up above that.

name: Snow
fact: Crystals grown by vapour freezing onto them, then stuck together. The aggregate is the snowflake that lands.

name: Storm
fact: Moisture, an unstable air mass, and something to lift it. Take one away and there is none.

name: Lightning
fact: Charge sorted by ice striking ice in the updraught, then let go all at once.

name: Thunder
fact: Air exploding away from a channel at about 30,000 K. Three seconds a kilometre.

name: Hail
fact: Ice laid down in layers at least a millimetre thick, held up by an updraught for half an hour or more.

name: Rainbow
fact: Always 42° out from the point opposite the sun. The geometry belongs to the drop.

name: Ozone
fact: O3, named for its smell — ozein, Greek for 'to smell'. It damages what it is named for.

name: Hurricane
fact: A storm that runs on warm water. Take it over sea much below 26.5 °C and it begins to die.

name: Blizzard
fact: Defined by wind, not by snowfall: 56 km/h or more, visibility down to 400 m, for three hours or more.

name: Flood
fact: Water arriving faster than the ground can absorb it or the channel can carry it.

name: Dune
fact: Sand that grew itself: sand hitting sand tends to stick, sand hitting hard ground bounces away.

name: Loess
fact: Wind-blown dust that landed and stayed. It weathers into some of the most productive farmland there is.

name: Fulgurite
fact: A glass tube left in the ground by a lightning strike, following the path the current took down.

name: Steel
fact: Iron with 0.02–2.14% carbon. The carbon jams the lattice so it cannot slip.

name: Bronze
fact: Copper with about an eighth part tin. Melts near 950 °C and casts far better than copper.

name: Brass
fact: Copper and zinc, roughly two to one. Change the ratio and you change the colour.

name: Solder
fact: A tin-lead mix that melts at 183 °C — lower than either metal on its own.

name: Hide
fact: Skin off the animal and untanned. Dries hard as board, and rots the moment it is wet again.

name: Tannin
fact: A plant polyphenol that grabs protein and drops it out of solution. Named for tanning.

name: Leather
fact: Tanned hide. Dries flexible instead of hard, and will not rot when it is wetted again.

name: Latex
fact: A milky colloid that runs from a cut in the bark. Rubber is suspended in it, not dissolved.

name: Rubber
fact: cis-1,4-polyisoprene, 100,000 to 1,000,000 daltons. Untreated, it goes sticky in heat.

name: Vulcanised rubber
fact: Rubber with sulfur chains stitched between its polymer strands. Goodyear, 1839.

name: Canvas
fact: Plain weave in heavy yarn. The word comes from cannabis — it used to be hemp.

name: Silkworm
fact: Bombyx mori has been bred until it cannot fly and does not exist in the wild.

name: Cocoon
fact: One unbroken filament, 300 to 900 metres of it, spun in about two or three days.

name: Silk
fact: A triangular fibre with rounded corners. It shines because it works like a prism.

name: Coin
fact: The first ones were electrum — a natural gold-silver alloy nobody could value by eye.

name: Nail
fact: Until about 1800 every one was forged singly by hand, and they were worth stealing.

name: Knife
fact: A blade and a tang running back into the handle, so the grip does not snap off it.

name: Needle
fact: The hard part was never the point. It was drilling an eye without splitting the bone.

name: Rope
fact: Every layer is twisted against the one below. That fight is the only thing holding it.

name: Wheel
fact: The potter's wheel came first. Cart wheels were plain wooden disks with a hole in them.

name: Lamp
fact: A pool of oil and a wick reaching down into it. Lascaux had one 15,000 years ago.

name: Shoe
fact: The oldest known one is 5,500 years old, one piece of hide, and its laces survived.

name: Pipe
fact: Plumbing is named after lead: plumbum. Soft enough to bend, and that was the problem.

name: Plough
fact: A share to cut the sod and a mouldboard to turn it over. Scratching the surface is not enough.

name: Peat
fact: Dead plants that could not rot, because mud or sour water kept the oxygen off them.

name: Coal
fact: Buried peat, squeezed and cooked for millions of years until mostly what is left is carbon.

name: Coal tar
fact: The black liquid that comes off coal heated without air. Phenol and cresols are in it.

name: Phenol
fact: An alcohol that behaves like an acid. Runge pulled the first of it out of coal tar in 1834.

name: Wood tar
fact: What drips out of wood heated without air, next to the charcoal that stays behind.

name: Methanol
fact: Wood alcohol. Boils at 64.7 °C, and 4 mL of it can take your sight permanently.

name: Formaldehyde
fact: It stitches proteins to each other. That is what fixing, embalming and smoke tanning all are.

name: Galalith
fact: Plastic made out of milk. Buttons, pen barrels and piano keys, from 1897 onwards.

name: Bakelite
fact: The first plastic made from synthetic parts. Baekeland, 1907. Once set it cannot be melted.

name: Ethanol
fact: Boils at 78.2 °C. Distilling stops at 95.6% — past that it and water boil as one thing.

name: Ethylene
fact: More of it is made than any other organic compound, and half of that becomes polythene.

name: Polyethylene
fact: The world's most used plastic, and it can be made from sugarcane instead of oil.

name: Magma
fact: Molten rock while it is still underground. Every igneous rock there is froze out of it.

name: Lava
fact: The same melt once it reaches the surface. Nothing changes but the address, and the name.

name: Basalt
fact: Fine, dark and everywhere: nearly the whole floor of every ocean is basalt.

name: Granite
fact: Quartz, feldspar and mica, grown big enough to see because the melt cooled slowly and deep.

name: Obsidian
fact: Volcanic glass. It froze too fast for one crystal to start, so it has no crystals at all.

name: Pumice
fact: Frozen volcanic froth, 64–85% holes by volume. It floats until it waterlogs and sinks.

name: Quartz
fact: Silicon dioxide. It outlasts every other mineral, which is why sand is mostly quartz.

name: Feldspar
fact: The commonest mineral group there is: about 41% of the continental crust by weight.

name: Mica
fact: A silicate built in sheets, bonded so weakly between them that it splits into elastic plates.

name: Sandstone
fact: Sand buried, squeezed and cemented. The grains are mostly quartz, because quartz survives.

name: Mudstone
fact: Mud turned to rock. Mudrocks are half of all the sedimentary rock in the record.

name: Shale
fact: Mudstone that splits: compaction lined its clay flakes up parallel, and it parts along them.

name: Conglomerate
fact: Rounded pebbles set in finer sediment. Only fast water shifts stones that size.

name: Slate
fact: Metamorphism, step one. It splits along the direction of the squeeze, not the old bedding.

name: Phyllite
fact: Between slate and schist. Its silky sheen is mica just large enough to catch the light.

name: Schist
fact: Mica grown big enough to see and all lying one way, so the rock splits into flakes.

name: Gneiss
fact: High grade, and striped: over 600 °C the pale and dark minerals sort into separate bands.

name: Marble
fact: Limestone recrystallised. The calcite grains grow and interlock, and the fossils go.

name: Quartzite
fact: Sandstone whose grains have fused. Break it and the crack runs through them, not around.

name: Lignite
fact: Brown coal: compressed peat, sometimes still three-quarters water. The lowest rank there is.

name: Anthracite
fact: The last rank of coal: 86–97% carbon, hard and glossy, with the tar cooked out of it.

name: Corundum
fact: Aluminium oxide, 9 on the Mohs scale. Pure it is colourless — the colours are impurities.

name: Diamond
fact: Carbon rearranged. It is stable only 150 km down, so every one you see was carried up.

name: Ruby
fact: Corundum with chromium standing in for a little of the aluminium. That alone makes it red.

name: Sapphire
fact: Corundum with iron and titanium. An electron hops between the pair and the stone reads blue.

name: Emerald
fact: Beryl coloured by chromium — the same element that makes ruby red, in a different crystal.

name: Opal
fact: Hydrated silica, 3–21% water, in spheres even enough to diffract light into colours.

name: Up Quark
fact: The lightest quark. Two of them and a down quark make every proton in the universe.

name: Down Quark
fact: Heavier than the up quark, and the reason a neutron is a neutron. Two downs and an up.

name: Proton
fact: Two up quarks and one down. Strip the electron off a hydrogen atom and this is what is left.

name: Neutron
fact: One up quark and two down. Outside a nucleus it lasts about fifteen minutes.

name: Electron
fact: 1/1836th the mass of a proton, and no known substructure. All of chemistry is these.

name: Atomic Nucleus
fact: Tens of thousands of times smaller than its atom, and almost all of the atom's mass.

name: Photon
fact: The quantum of the electromagnetic field. Massless, and it only ever travels at one speed.

name: Gamma Ray
fact: The same stuff as light, at a million times the energy. Lead and concrete, not paper.

name: Plasma
fact: Gas with its electrons torn off. An estimated 99.9% of ordinary matter is in this state.

name: Deuterium
fact: Hydrogen with a neutron. About 156 atoms in every million of the hydrogen in seawater.

name: Tritium
fact: Hydrogen with two neutrons. Radioactive, half-life 12.32 years, so none of it is original.

name: Fission Products
fact: The two halves a split nucleus leaves. Caesium-137 and strontium-90 both take 30 years to halve.

name: Cosmic Dust
fact: Grains from a few molecules up to 0.1 mm, condensed in the winds of dying stars.

name: Nebula
fact: A luminous patch of the interstellar medium — hydrogen and dust, and where stars come from.

name: Star
fact: A luminous spheroid of plasma held together by its own gravity. Nothing else is required.

name: Red Giant
fact: A star that has run out of core hydrogen and swollen. The Sun will do this in 5 billion years.

name: White Dwarf
fact: A dead core the size of Earth with the mass of the Sun. One tonne per cubic centimetre.

name: Supernova
fact: Several solar masses thrown outward at three per cent of the speed of light.

name: Neutron Star
fact: 1.4 solar masses in a 10 km ball. A matchbox of it would weigh about 3 billion tonnes.

name: Black Hole
fact: Gravity so strong that nothing, light included, can cross back out of the event horizon.

name: Planetesimal
fact: A solid body about a kilometre across — big enough that its own gravity holds it together.

name: Planet
fact: Round under its own gravity, and it has swept its orbit clear. Both halves matter.

name: Moon
fact: Made from the debris of a Mars-sized body hitting the Earth about 4.4 billion years ago.

name: Comet
fact: Rock, dust and frozen water, carbon dioxide, methane and ammonia. A dirty snowball.

name: Asteroid
fact: The whole belt weighs 3% of the Moon. Jupiter threw out over 99% of what was there.

name: Gas Giant
fact: Mostly hydrogen and helium — over 90% by mass. Jupiter and Saturn are the two here.

name: Ice Giant
fact: Only about 20% hydrogen and helium. The rest is water, ammonia and methane.

name: Bacteria
fact: DNA loose in the cytoplasm, no nucleus, no organelles. The other, older way to be a cell.

name: Archaea
fact: A third domain, separated from bacteria in 1977. Its membranes use a chemistry nothing else does.

name: Mitochondrion
fact: It keeps its own circular DNA and its own bacterial ribosomes, because it used to be a bacterium.

name: Chloroplast
fact: A cyanobacterium that moved into a cell two billion years ago and never came out again.

name: Cyanobacteria
fact: The first organisms known to have produced oxygen, and they filled the whole sky with it.

name: Alga
fact: Photosynthetic, and mostly single-celled, with no roots, leaves or stems. Not one family.

name: Fungus
fact: Neither plant nor animal. It digests its food outside its own body, then absorbs the result.

name: Spore
fact: One cell that can build a whole fungus. Most fungal spores are carried by the wind.

name: Mycelium
fact: The actual fungus: branching threads through soil. One can span thousands of acres.

name: Lichen
fact: A fungus and an alga living as one thing. Under some conditions that counts as parasitism.

name: Mycorrhiza
fact: Fungus fused to root. Found in 92% of plant families, and at least 460 million years old.

name: Root Nodule
fact: A lump on a legume root, red inside, housing bacteria the plant lets in and then feeds.

name: Rhizobium
fact: A soil bacterium the legume lets inside. In the nodule it starts breaking nitrogen apart.

name: Ammonia
fact: NH3. Nearly every nitrogen atom in a living thing entered biology through this molecule.

name: Pollen
fact: Not a sperm cell but a whole small organism, in a wall tough enough to survive fossilisation.

name: Coral Polyp
fact: A sac two cell layers thick with one opening, and that opening is both mouth and exit.

name: Zooxanthellae
fact: Single-celled algae living inside an animal's own cells, in vacuoles, paying rent in sugar.

name: Coral
fact: An animal taking up to 90% of its food from the algae growing inside its own tissue.

name: Coral Reef
fact: Under 0.1% of the ocean's area, and home to at least a quarter of all marine species.

name: Atoll
fact: A ring of reef around a lagoon. The island it grew on sank, and the coral grew upward to keep pace.

name: Bleached Coral
fact: White because the algae have gone. The animal is not dead yet; it is starving.

name: Detritus
fact: Dead plant matter in pieces. More material goes down this chain than through anything's mouth.

name: Earthworm
fact: Breathes through its skin, so it needs damp soil — and so rain does not drown it.

name: Humus
fact: The dark residue when decay runs out of easy food. Much of it has sat there over a century.

name: Compost
fact: A heap gets hot without being lit: 54–71 °C, all of it waste heat from microbes eating.

name: Cellulose
fact: Glucose chained with the bond flipped. The most abundant organic polymer on Earth.

name: Rumen
fact: The largest stomach compartment in a ruminant, and it holds no cellulase of the cow's own.

name: Volatile Fatty Acid
fact: Acetate, propionate, butyrate. A cow's actual food, made for it by something else.

name: Lodestone
fact: Magnetite that a lightning strike magnetised. The Earth's own field is far too weak to do it.

name: Magnet
fact: Stroke iron with a lodestone and its domains line up. Hard iron keeps the alignment; soft iron loses it.

name: Magnetic field
fact: The region where a magnet or a current pushes. Iron filings on paper lie along its lines.

name: Copper wire
fact: Copper pulled cold through a die. It gets longer as it gets thinner, and never loses volume.

name: Voltaic pile
fact: Volta, 1800: zinc and copper discs stacked with brine-soaked card. The first steady current.

name: Generator
fact: Faraday's disk, 1831. Spin a conductor through a field and the field pays back in current.

name: Electric current
fact: A flow of charge. In a copper wire the electrons drift about a millimetre a second.

name: Electromagnet
fact: A coil around iron. Its field can be thousands of times the coil's alone, and it switches off.

name: Electric motor
fact: A field pushes sideways on a current. The commutator flips the current so it keeps pushing.

name: Transformer
fact: Two coils on one iron ring. Voltage out over voltage in is just the ratio of the turns.

name: Nichrome
fact: 80% nickel, 20% chromium: 66 times the resistivity of copper, and it will not burn away.

name: Heating element
fact: A resistor whose whole job is to waste power. Heat goes as current squared times resistance.

name: Filament
fact: A coil of a coil, so the hot gas only ever flows past the outside of it.

name: Light bulb
fact: A wire held at 2,500 °C in gas that will not react with it. Most of what leaves is heat.

name: Sulfuric acid
fact: The most-made industrial chemical. It pulls water out of things, including skin.

name: Lead-acid cell
fact: Planté, 1859 — the first battery you could refill with current instead of throw away.

name: Electrolysis
fact: Push current through a solution and you can drive a reaction backwards, uphill.

name: Electroplating
fact: Metal taken off one electrode and put back on another, an atom at a time.

name: P-type silicon
fact: Silicon with boron in it. Boron is one electron short, so the gaps do the carrying.

name: N-type silicon
fact: Silicon with phosphorus in it. Phosphorus has one electron spare and lets it go.

name: Diode
fact: Two doped silicons meeting. Charge crosses the seam one way and not the other.

name: LED
fact: Electrons falling into holes. The size of the gap they fall across sets the colour.

name: Transistor
fact: A small current at one terminal ruling a large one at another. Everything modern sits on it.

name: Solar cell
fact: A diode in the light. The junction's field pulls the pair apart before they recombine.

name: Refrigerator
fact: It does not make cold. It carries heat out of the box and dumps it behind the box.

name: Thyroxine
fact: Two tyrosine rings joined, carrying four iodine atoms. T3 is the same molecule one iodine lighter.

name: Ascorbate
fact: Vitamin C. Plants reach it from glucose by way of L-galactose; animals take another road from the same sugar.

name: Hydroxyproline
fact: Proline given a hydroxyl after the chain was already built. Collagen is full of it.

name: Triple Helix
fact: Three left-handed strands twisted into one right-handed rope, 3.3 residues to a turn.

name: Hydroxyapatite
fact: Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 — 65 to 70% of the mass of bone, and more of tooth enamel.

name: Fluorapatite
fact: Hydroxyapatite with fluoride sitting where the hydroxide was. Harder, and slower to give way to acid.

name: Porphyrin
fact: Four pyrrole rings closed into a circle, four nitrogens pointing inward at a hole sized for one metal ion.

name: Heme
fact: A porphyrin with an iron ion held in the middle. It carries oxygen, moves electrons and senses gas.

name: Haemoglobin
fact: Four chains, four hemes, four oxygens — and it lifts blood's oxygen capacity seventyfold.

name: Myoglobin
fact: One chain, one heme, and a firmer grip on oxygen than haemoglobin has.

name: Chlorophyll
fact: Heme's ring with magnesium instead of iron. It is a poor absorber of green, which is why leaves are.

name: Cobalamin
fact: Vitamin B12: a corrin ring around a cobalt ion. Only archaea and bacteria can build one.

name: Photosystem II
fact: Four manganese ions and one calcium in a single cluster, counting to four so water can be split.

name: Iron-Sulfur Cluster
fact: Iron and sulfide at the corners of a cube, tied to the protein by cysteines.

name: Cytochrome c Oxidase
fact: Two hemes and two coppers. The last enzyme in the respiratory electron transport chain.

name: Ferritin
fact: A hollow protein sphere of 24 parts, holding about 4,500 iron ions where they can catalyse nothing.

name: Zinc Finger
fact: A loop too small to hold its own shape until a zinc ion pins it. Then it reads DNA.

name: Carbonic Anhydrase
fact: One zinc ion, and up to a million reactions a second — ten million times faster than no enzyme at all.

name: Selenocysteine
fact: The 21st amino acid, spelled with a stop codon. Cysteine with selenium where the sulfur was.

name: Glutathione Peroxidase
fact: A selenoprotein. Its selenium is the atom hydrogen peroxide reacts with first.

name: Sulfite Oxidase
fact: Carries molybdenum on a pterin ring, in the gap between the two mitochondrial membranes.

name: Superoxide Dismutase
fact: Works as fast as molecules can collide. Built around copper, manganese, iron or nickel.

name: Sodium-Potassium Pump
fact: Three sodium out, two potassium in, one ATP. A nerve cell can spend most of its energy on this.

name: Action Potential
fact: Sodium in, potassium out. Almost no ions actually move, and the voltage swings anyway.

name: Retinal
fact: Half a beta-carotene, cut down the middle. The molecule that absorbs the light you see by.

name: Rhodopsin
fact: A protein wrapped round one retinal. A photon straightens the retinal, and seeing starts there.

name: Magnesium Oxide
fact: What is left after the flash. Prized as a refractory — it holds where other furnace linings fail.

name: Zinc Oxide
fact: The alchemists' philosopher's wool: white fume off burning zinc, caught and collected.

name: Copper Oxide
fact: Black powder that fires blue, green or red in a glaze, depending on what the kiln does.

name: Rust
fact: Iron's failure mode. Flaky, friable, and offering the metal underneath no protection at all.

name: Litharge
fact: Lead's oxide. Red below 486 °C, yellow above it — one compound, two crystal packings.

name: Mercuric Oxide
fact: The red powder that gave up oxygen to Priestley in 1774, before the gas had a name.

name: Alumina
fact: A film of this about 5 nm thick is the only reason aluminium looks unreactive.

name: Copper Sulfide
fact: Chalcocite in the ground. Most of the world's copper is roasted out of this.

name: Zinc Sulfide
fact: Doped with a trace of metal it glows when struck. The first particle detector was a screen of it.

name: Lead Sulfide
fact: Galena. The main lead-bearing mineral, and mostly found sitting with zinc ores.

name: Tarnish
fact: The black on old silver is not oxide. Silver ignores air; it is sulfur it cannot ignore.

name: Potassium Chloride
fact: The other salt. Most of it goes on fields as potash; the rest into low-sodium table salt.

name: Potassium Iodide
fact: What the word 'iodised' on a salt packet means. A few parts per million, against deficiency.

name: Sodium Fluoride
fact: Trace amounts in water and toothpaste turn tooth enamel into fluorapatite.

name: Hydrogen Chloride
fact: A gas until it meets water, and then it is hydrochloric acid — one of the strong ones.

name: Tungsten Carbide
fact: As hard as corundum and close to diamond. The tip of the tool that cuts the steel.

name: Calcium Carbide
fact: A rock that makes a flammable gas when it gets wet. It lit mines for fifty years.

name: Acetylene
fact: Burnt with oxygen it passes 3,300 °C — the hottest flame any common gas pair makes.

name: Titanium Nitride
fact: Brown as a powder, gold as a coating. The colour on a drill bit is hardness, not paint.

name: Magnesium Nitride
fact: Proof that a magnesium fire does not care about oxygen: it burns in pure nitrogen too.

name: Carbon Monoxide
fact: Colourless, odourless, flammable. The commonest fatal air poisoning in many countries.

name: Sulfur Dioxide
fact: The smell of a struck match. Volcanic eruptions are the largest source of it there is.

name: Hydrogen Sulfide
fact: Rotten eggs, briefly. It paralyses the nerve that smells it, and then you cannot.

name: Nitric Oxide
fact: What lightning makes out of air. Colourless, and not for long once it meets oxygen.

name: Nitrogen Dioxide
fact: The brown in a bad city sky. Nitric oxide plus one more oxygen atom.

name: Nitrate
fact: The form a root can actually take nitrogen up in. Almost all of them dissolve in water.

name: Phosphate
fact: PO4 — one phosphorus, four oxygens. It bridges DNA's sugars and it is what ATP spends.

name: Ribose
fact: The five-carbon sugar in RNA. Glucose becomes it by the pentose phosphate pathway.

name: Deoxyribose
fact: Ribose minus one oxygen. That missing hydroxyl is the whole difference between RNA and DNA.

name: Adenine
fact: The A. Also the business end of ATP — the cell spells with it and pays with it.

name: Guanine
fact: Named from guano, isolated from bird droppings in 1844. The crystals also make fish scales shine.

name: Cytosine
fact: The C. Unstable enough that it turns into uracil on its own, which is why DNA has a repair crew.

name: Thymine
fact: 5-methyluracil: uracil with one methyl group. DNA uses it where RNA uses uracil.

name: Uracil
fact: RNA's U. Found in the Murchison meteorite, and in 2023 in a sample from the asteroid Ryugu.

name: Base Pair
fact: A with T by two hydrogen bonds, G with C by three. That is the whole copying mechanism.

name: RNA
fact: One strand, ribose, uracil. Chemically the more fragile of the two, and probably the older.

name: Transfer RNA
fact: 76 to 90 nucleotides. Reads a codon at one end and holds an amino acid at the other.

name: Ribosomal RNA
fact: About 60% of the ribosome by mass, and the part that does the chemistry.

name: Ribozyme
fact: RNA that catalyses. Cech and Altman took the 1989 Nobel for finding RNA could do that at all.

name: Phospholipid
fact: A phosphate head and two greasy tails. In water it builds a bilayer with no help at all.

name: Cholesterol
fact: An animal molecule that stiffens or loosens a membrane. Most of yours is made, not eaten.

name: Vesicle
fact: A bubble of bilayer with water inside. The cheapest inside there is.

name: Primordial Soup
fact: Oparin's 1924 guess at the early ocean. Haldane supplied the word soup in 1929.

name: Protocell
fact: A bilayer sac with replicating chemistry inside. Nobody has yet made one that lives.

name: Cytoplasm
fact: About 80% water, and so crowded with protein that nothing dissolved in it behaves normally.

name: Virus
fact: A genome in a protein coat, with no metabolism. Called organisms at the edge of life.

name: Binary Fission
fact: One cell into two, no partner. E. coli does it about every 20 minutes at 37 °C.

name: Budding
fact: The daughter grows out of the mother's side and leaves. Yeast does it; so does a hydra.

name: Cutting
fact: A severed stem that grows its own roots. The new plant is a clone of the one it came off.

name: Tuber
fact: A potato is not a root. It is a swollen underground stem, and every eye on it is a bud.

name: Runner
fact: A stolon: a stem that crawls sideways and roots where it touches. Strawberries spread this way.

name: Glycogen
fact: Starch's animal counterpart, branched far more. About 100 g in the liver, 400 g in muscle.

name: Methane
fact: CH4, the simplest alkane. Some archaea make it, and nothing else alive does.

name: Cactus
fact: Spines are modified leaves; the fat stem does the photosynthesis. Water can be 90% of its mass.

name: Malic Acid
fact: A four-carbon acid. CAM plants build it in the dark and take it apart again in the light.

name: Stoma
fact: A pore between two guard cells. Opening it to eat costs the plant water, every single time.

name: Xylem
fact: Dead pipework. Wood is xylem that kept being added, one year's worth at a time.

name: Phloem
fact: Living tissue, unlike xylem. It carries sugar downward, and it sits just inside the bark.

name: Sap
fact: Two saps, running opposite ways. Neither of them is latex, and neither of them is resin.

name: Bark
fact: Everything outside the vascular cambium. Strip a ring of it off and the tree usually dies.

name: Cork
fact: Dead cells full of gas, walled with suberin. Stripped off a living oak, and it grows back.

name: Lignin
fact: 20 to 35% of dry wood. Stiffens the cell wall, keeps water in the pipes, and resists rot.

name: Oak
fact: Around 500 species. The tannin that makes acorns bitter is the tannin that tanned leather.

name: Pine
fact: Evergreen and resinous. Over 90% of a conifer's timber is one cell type: the tracheid.

name: Hardwood
fact: Wood from a flowering tree, with vessels. Balsa is one, so the name is not about hardness.

name: Softwood
fact: Wood from a conifer, with no pores at all. Yew is a softwood and harder than many hardwoods.

name: Bamboo
fact: A grass. Some species add 91 cm in a day, and a culm never gets thicker than it started.

name: Coconut
fact: A drupe, not a nut. The husk is built for buoyancy, but people did most of the carrying.

name: Coconut Water
fact: Liquid endosperm — the same tissue that later settles out as the solid white flesh.

name: Mangrove
fact: Filters salt out at the root and dumps the rest in old leaves. Its seeds sprout on the tree.

name: Bast Fibre
fact: Fibre out of the inner bark. Soft and flexible, unlike the stiff leaf fibres of sisal.

name: Sugar Beet
fact: A taproot that is 12 to 21% sucrose. Breeding took it from 8% to 18% in two centuries.

name: Rubber Tree
fact: Amazonian, and barely grown there: a leaf blight keeps plantations out of its own homeland.

name: Mulberry
fact: In the fig's family. What looks like one fruit is many fruits packed against each other.

name: Willow
fact: Roots from a broken branch lying on wet ground. Its bark sap is rich in salicin.

name: Salicin
fact: Bitter as quinine. The gut turns it into salicylic acid — the compound aspirin was built on.

name: Winter Wheat
fact: Sown in autumn. It will not flower until weeks of 1–7 °C have switched off its FLC repressor.

name: Gibberellin
fact: A growth hormone, found first in a fungus that made rice grow too tall to hold itself up.

name: Semi-Dwarf Wheat
fact: Norin 10's Rht1 and Rht2, crossed in by Borlaug. Short straw, heavy head, and it stays upright.

name: Graft
fact: Cambium pressed to cambium. The top keeps its own genes, so the fruit is the scion's.

name: Phytochrome
fact: A light sensor built from a cracked-open haem ring. Red switches it on, far-red switches it back.

name: Foxglove
fact: Rosette one year, spire the next, then dead. Leaves, flowers and seeds all carry the poison.

name: Digoxin
fact: Isolated in 1930 from the woolly foxglove, not the garden one. It blocks the sodium-potassium pump.

name: Capsicum
fact: One species. Capsaicin sits in the white pith the seeds hang off, not in the seeds themselves.

name: Paprika
fact: Dried mild Capsicum annuum, ground. Red from carotenoids; as extract E160c it colours food.

name: Pectin
fact: The glue between plant cells. Ripening enzymes cut it, and that is why fruit goes soft.

name: Lanolin
fact: The grease sheep secrete to keep rain out of their fleece. Washed from the wool, it goes into ointments.

name: Tallow
fact: Rendered beef or mutton suet. Solid at room temperature, and it keeps for months without a fridge.

name: Horn
fact: A keratin sheath over a living bone core. Grown for life and never shed, which an antler is not.

name: Antler
fact: Solid bone, grown and dropped every year. No other mammal bone grows faster.

name: Feather
fact: Beta-keratin grown from a follicle. Barbs hook to barbs with tiny barbicels to make an airtight vane.

name: Down
fact: The under-layer with no hooks on its barbules, so it traps air instead of making a flight surface.

name: Oyster
fact: A filter feeder that builds its own stone house. One can pull 190 litres of water through its gills a day.

name: Pearl
fact: Nacre wrapped around an intruder by the mantle. Rarely the grain of sand of the story.

name: Nacre
fact: Aragonite tablets half a micrometre thick, stacked in protein. That thickness is why it shimmers.

name: Lac insect
fact: A scale insect that settles on a twig, feeds on sap, and coats the whole branch in resin.

name: Shellac
fact: Insect resin melted, filtered and flaked. Dissolved in alcohol it is a varnish; pressed, it was a record.

name: Cochineal
fact: A scale insect farmed on prickly pear. Up to a quarter of its dried weight is red dye.

name: Carmine
fact: Carminic acid locked to aluminium. The red in yoghurt, sweets and lipstick, and a real allergen.

name: Rennet
fact: Chymosin from the fourth stomach of an unweaned calf — the enzyme that sets milk into curd.

name: Whey
fact: What runs off the cut curd: water, lactose, and the milk proteins rennet leaves alone.

name: Ricotta
fact: Recooked. Heat coagulates the whey proteins that rennet could not touch.

name: Swim bladder
fact: A gas bag that holds a fish at depth without swimming. It is the same organ as a lung.

name: Isinglass
fact: Dried fish swim bladder, nearly pure collagen. It drags the yeast out of beer.

name: Roe
fact: The ripe egg mass of a fish. A single salmon redd can hold five thousand of them.

name: Whale
fact: A mammal that went back to the sea. It breathes air and feeds its calf milk the thickness of paste.

name: Ambergris
fact: Sperm whale gut secretion, weathered at sea for years until it stops smelling foul.

name: Baleen
fact: Keratin plates that strain krill out of a mouthful of sea. Called whalebone, and it is not bone.

name: Ox
fact: A castrated bull trained to pull. Calm, heavy and steady all day — the engine before engines.

name: Manure
fact: Most of the nitrogen a grazing animal eats leaves again in the dung, ready for the next crop.

name: Parchment
fact: Limed skin dried under tension, never tanned. It buckles whenever the air turns damp.

name: Sinew
fact: Tendon: collagen all lined up one way. Enormously strong along it, useless across it.

name: Ivory
fact: Dentine from a tusk that never stopped growing. Polished, it shows a crosshatch nothing else has.

name: Royal jelly
fact: Fed to a larva for the whole of its growth, it makes a queen out of a would-be worker.

name: S. thermophilus
fact: Named heat-liking, and it means it: best growth 35–42 °C. Turns milk's lactose into lactic acid.

name: L. bulgaricus
fact: Isolated from Bulgarian yoghurt in 1905 and named for the country. Grows best at 40–44 °C.

name: L. acidophilus
fact: Acid-loving, literally: grows most readily below pH 5. A gut and mouth organism, not a milk one.

name: Bifidobacterium
fact: Branched and Y-shaped — bifid — and anaerobic. The commonest bacterium in an infant's gut.

name: L. paracasei
fact: Not a starter. It arrives later, grows in ripening cheese, and takes the proteins apart as it goes.

name: L. plantarum
fact: The plant one. Grows anywhere from pH 3.4 to 8.8, and at 15 °C but not at 45.

name: Leuconostoc
fact: Lives on the skins of fruit and vegetables. Heterofermentative: it gives off CO₂ as well as acid.

name: Lactococcus
fact: The cheese and buttermilk bacterium. Dairy strains are plant strains that shed the genes milk made useless.

name: Acetobacter
fact: Turns ethanol into acetic acid, and needs oxygen to do it. Pasteur found the first one in 1864.

name: Penicillium
fact: A soil mould of cool climates, over 300 species. One of them is why there is antibiotic in this game.

name: Koji
fact: Aspergillus oryzae grown on steamed grain. Its aflatoxin genes are still there and no longer work.

name: Kefir Grains
fact: Not an organism: bacteria and yeasts living in a matrix of the polysaccharide kefiran.

name: Lactic Acid
fact: What homofermentative bacteria make from glucose: two lactate, two ATP, and no gas at all.

name: Acetic Acid
fact: The sour in vinegar. Freezes to ice-like crystals just below room temperature, at 16.6 °C.

name: Yoghurt Culture
fact: Each feeds the other: amino acids from milk protein one way, folic and formic acid the other.

name: Starter Culture
fact: The culture that actually performs the fermentation, kept alive off the food by freeze-drying.

name: Pasteurised Milk
fact: Heated enough to kill the pathogens and not enough to sterilise. Most bacterial spores come through.

name: Souring Kraut
fact: Phase two in the crock: Leuconostoc has taken dominance, and the gas coming off is its doing.

name: Kefir
fact: Sour, fizzy and faintly alcoholic — because yeasts ferment it alongside the bacteria.

name: Buttermilk
fact: What is left in the churn after souring the cream. Under 0.5 per cent fat.

name: Miso
fact: Soybeans, salt and koji, left until the mould's enzymes have taken the beans apart.

name: Camembert
fact: Ripened from the rind inwards by a mould sprayed on the outside, for at least three weeks.

name: Beef
fact: Cattle's meat. Beef and cow run back to one Indo-European root by two different roads.

name: Pork
fact: The pig's meat, and the second most eaten meat in the world after poultry.

name: Mutton
fact: A sheep past two years old. Tougher than lamb, and darker — colour tracks age.

name: Lamb
fact: A sheep in its first year, and its meat. One English word does both jobs.

name: Venison
fact: From Latin venari, to hunt. It once meant the meat of anything hunted, not only deer.

name: Calf
fact: A dairy cow has to calve to keep milking, so a dairy makes calves whether it wants them or not.

name: Veal
fact: The meat of a calf. Mostly the dairy's male calves, which will never give milk.

name: Poultry
fact: Domesticated birds kept for meat, eggs or feathers. A wild bird shot for the pot is game.

name: Game
fact: Not a species but a status: wild animals hunted for meat, and leaner than farmed ones.

name: Steak
fact: Cut from the loin, which barely works. Tenderness rises with distance from hoof and horn.

name: Aged Beef
fact: Held near freezing for weeks while the meat's own enzymes take its connective tissue apart.

name: Ham
fact: The pig's hind leg, cured. Ham is Old English for the bend of the knee, gammon the French for it.

name: Stew
fact: Slow, moist heat for the least tender cuts. The juiciness is collagen, not added water.

name: Carob
