fact: A Mediterranean legume that grows as an evergreen tree. The carat is named after its seed.

name: Locust bean gum
fact: E410. The milled endosperm of a carob seed — 42 to 46% of the seed, and mostly galactomannan.

name: Guar gum
fact: E412. Ground guar-bean endosperm, with about eight times the thickening power of cornstarch.

name: Xanthan gum
fact: E415. Secreted by Xanthomonas campestris, the bacterium that causes black rot in cabbages.

name: Red alga
fact: Rhodophyta. Red from phycobilin pigments, and the source of both agar and carrageenan.

name: Carrageenan
fact: E407. Sulfated galactose chains from red seaweed. Kappa gels with potassium and grips milk protein.

name: Agar
fact: E406. Sets at 32–42 °C and will not melt again below 85 — a gap gelatin does not have.

name: Alginate
fact: E401. Out of brown seaweed. Drop a solution of it into calcium and it gels on contact.

name: Citric acid
fact: E330. Nearly all of it is grown, not squeezed — a mould fed on sugar, since 1919.

name: Sodium acetate
fact: E262. Vinegar's acid, neutralised — a stable solid that holds food at a mildly acidic pH.

name: MSG
fact: E621. The sodium salt of glutamate. Ikeda pulled it out of kombu in 1908 and named the taste umami.

name: Inosinate
fact: E631. A nucleotide that meat and fish already carry at 80 to 800 mg per 100 g.

name: Guanylate
fact: E627. The salt of GMP. Expensive, and almost never used unless glutamate is already there.

name: Ribonucleotides
fact: E635. Inosinate and guanylate mixed. Two per cent of it in MSG quadruples the effect.

name: Maltodextrin
fact: Starch cut short — three to seventeen glucose units. Past DE 20 the same stuff is glucose syrup.

name: Hydrolysed protein
fact: Plant protein taken apart into free amino acids. Where the loose glutamate in savoury food comes from.

name: Silicon dioxide
fact: E551. Amorphous silica, not quartz — a branched powder that is nearly all surface.

name: Beta-carotene
fact: E160a. The orange in a carrot, and one molecule of it is cut in the gut into two of vitamin A.

name: Annatto
fact: E160b. Achiote seed. The colour sits in a waxy coat on the outside of the seed, not inside it.

name: Turmeric
fact: A rhizome in the ginger family. It cannot seed itself — every plant is a piece of another.

name: Curcumin
fact: E100. Turmeric's yellow. It barely dissolves in water and goes readily into alcohol or oil.

name: Betanin
fact: E162. Beetroot red — a betalain, which carries nitrogen. No plant makes betalains and anthocyanins both.

name: Caramel colour
fact: E150. Sugar cooked with acid, alkali or salt until brown. More fully oxidised than caramel candy.

name: Ponceau 4R
fact: E124. A synthetic azo dye, built from aromatic rings. Azo dyes do not occur in nature at all.

name: Sorbate
fact: E200–203. Named for the rowan it was distilled from in 1859. Now essentially all synthetic.

name: Benzoate
fact: E210–213. Named after gum benzoin, made now from toluene, and it only works in acidic food.

name: Sulfite
fact: E220–228. Sulfur dioxide taken onto a salt. In wine it stops fermentation and blocks oxidation.

name: Nitrite
fact: E249–250. It turns cured meat pink and holds back the spores that make botulinum toxin.

name: Hydrogenated oil
fact: Liquid oil with hydrogen added across its double bonds, so it sets solid. Normann's patent, 1902.

name: Trans fat
fact: A side reaction nobody wanted. Partial hydrogenation flips cis double bonds to trans as it goes.

name: Monoglyceride
fact: E471. A triglyceride with two of its three fatty acids gone, so one end will accept water.

name: Lecithin
fact: E322. Named from lekithos, the Greek for egg yolk, where Gobley found it in 1845.

name: Sorbitol
fact: E420. Glucose with its aldehyde end reduced to an alcohol. About half as sweet as sugar.

name: Xylitol
fact: E967. Wood sugar, reduced. Xylan out of timber, acid-split to xylose, then hydrogenated.

name: Aspartame
fact: E951. Two amino acids joined and capped with a methyl ester. About 200 times as sweet as sugar.

name: Peanut
fact: A legume, not a nut. It flowers above ground and then drives a stalk down to ripen its pods underground.

name: Sesame
fact: Its capsules burst when the seed is ripe and scatter it. Cereals were bred out of that habit; sesame was not.

name: Almond
fact: Nearly half the honeybee hives in the US are trucked to California each February, for this one crop.

name: Drupe
fact: Stone fruit. The stone is hardened ovary wall, not seed coat — and that test rules out most nuts.

name: Mango
fact: A drupe in the cashew family. Its skin and sap carry the oil that makes poison ivy poison ivy.

name: Urushiol
fact: The oil in poison ivy. Also in mango skin, leaves and sap, and in the shell of a raw cashew.

name: Sumac
fact: A whole dried fruit, ground. Sour from malic acid, and Rome used it where we now use lemon.

name: Walnut
fact: Not a true nut, and not quite a drupe. The shell is the stone; the green husk is not part of the fruit.

name: Juglone
fact: 2–4% of a fresh walnut husk. Stains hands brown and stops other plants growing under the tree.

name: Black Pepper
fact: A vine's unripe drupe. It is cooked before drying, and that is why the corn goes black.

name: Piperine
fact: Pepper's heat. It opens the same channel capsaicin does, from a plant that is no relation.

name: Jalapeño
fact: A pod type, not a species. Same plant as the sweet bell pepper, picked green and hotter if left red.

name: Chipotle
fact: A smoked red jalapeño. Ten pounds of fresh pepper go in and one pound comes out.

name: Cumin
fact: The seed is a whole dried fruit. Same family as carrot, celery, parsley and dill.

name: Marjoram
fact: Origanum majorana. Oregano is the other species in the genus, and its other name is wild marjoram.

name: Lime
fact: The Navy swapped lemon for lime and scurvy came back. Lime juice is the far weaker cure.

name: Makrut Lime
fact: The leaf is the crop, not the fruit. It looks like two leaves because the stalk is winged.

name: Rhizome
fact: A stem that runs sideways underground. It has nodes and buds; a root has neither.

name: Ginger
fact: A rhizome, not a root, and turmeric's close relative. No wild form is left — every plant is a cutting.

name: Gingerol
fact: Fresh ginger's heat: a yellow oil in the rhizome. Drying wrecks it into something hotter.

name: Shogaol
fact: 160,000 Scoville. Why dried ginger bites harder than fresh — it is not the same molecule.

name: Celery
fact: The strings are collenchyma, bundled outside the veins. A marsh umbellifer, like carrot and cumin.

name: Raisin
fact: A grape resists drying. Its skin is waxed against water loss, which is the whole difficulty.

name: Lentil
fact: The optical lens is named after this seed, not the other way round. Latin lens meant lentil first.

name: Split Pea
fact: It splits where it was always going to: down the seam between its two cotyledons.

name: Farro
fact: Not one grain. Einkorn, emmer or spelt — hulled wheats that will not thresh clean.

name: Sunflower
fact: Mature heads do not follow the sun. They stop, facing east, and the morning warmth brings pollinators.

name: Oil
fact: Generic vegetable oil. Deodorised at 232 °C, which is why the bottle need not name a plant.

name: Vitamin A
fact: Retinol. One reduction step from retinal, and the liver stores it as an ester until asked.

name: Vitamin D
fact: Not a vitamin. UVB builds it in your skin from a cholesterol precursor, so it is a hormone you make.

name: Soy Sauce
fact: Koji, brine and months. 17–20% salt, so only the halophiles get to work.

name: Candied Fruit
fact: Sugar traded for water, a little stronger each week, until nothing can grow in it.

name: Coconut Sugar
fact: Tapped from the cut flower stem, not the nut. Sap that is 80% water, boiled down.

name: Parsley
fact: Parsley seed holds apiol in enough quantity to be toxic — the leaf everyone eats does not.

name: Sage
fact: Its oil contains thujone, a neurotoxin that can cause convulsions in high enough doses.

name: Rosemary
fact: Its name means 'dew of the sea' in Latin, and it grows wild on cliffs above the Mediterranean.

name: Basil
fact: Its name means 'royal plant' — from the Greek basilikón phytón, kingly herb.

name: Thyme
fact: Thymol, its antiseptic oil, is the same compound now used as an active ingredient in Listerine.

name: Mint
fact: A sterile hybrid of watermint and spearmint. It cannot set seed — every plant grows from a runner.

name: Tarragon
fact: Named for its coiled roots — Latin dracunculus, 'little dragon'. French tarragon can't be grown from seed.

name: Dill
fact: Its scent comes from carvone — flip the molecule to its mirror image and you get spearmint instead.

name: Coriander
fact: A gene variant, OR6A2, makes some people taste soap instead of citrus in the leaf.

name: Chives
fact: Its sulfur compounds repel most insects, but the flowers still draw bees in to pollinate.

name: Bay Leaf
fact: Comes from an evergreen tree that can reach 20 metres — most kitchen herbs aren't trees at all.

name: Oregano
fact: Gets stronger when dried, not weaker — the opposite of almost every other kitchen herb.

name: Thiamin
fact: The first vitamin ever isolated — pulled from rice bran in 1910, the layer polishing removes.

name: Riboflavin
fact: The reason whey glows yellow-green — first isolated from it in 1879, called lactochrome.

name: Niacin
fact: Your body makes it from tryptophan at a steep, fixed rate: 60 milligrams in for 1 milligram out.

name: Folate
fact: Named for the Latin word for leaf — first isolated by extracting it from spinach in 1941.

name: Vitamin B6
fact: Plants build it partly as their own sunscreen, a defence against UV-B. Animals never gained that trick.

name: Vitamin E
fact: Named tocopherol, Greek for 'to bear a child' — discovered in 1922 as the fertility factor rats needed.

name: Red 40
fact: Invented in 1971 to replace amaranth, the red dye the FDA later banned for causing cancer.

name: Yellow 5
fact: A 2024 discovery: this yellow dye can turn live mouse skin briefly transparent under light.

name: Yellow 6
fact: Mixed with red dye amaranth to fake the brown of chocolate and caramel. Made from petroleum.

name: Blue 1
fact: The same blue candy dye is also poured into rivers and soil to trace how water moves.

name: Gum Arabic
fact: E414. Tapped from Acacia bark, from which the gum exudes on its own.

name: Gellan Gum
fact: E418. About half the concentration of agar reaches the same gel strength.

name: Arrowroot
fact: Its fine grain once made it a standard ingredient in carbonless copy paper.

name: Shiitake
fact: Traditionally grown on cut logs set beside trees already carrying its spores.

name: Maitake
fact: Called 'dancing mushroom' in Japanese; grows in clumps at the base of old oak trees.

name: Spirulina
fact: Not algae or a plant — it's dried cyanobacterium biomass, farmed in alkaline ponds.

name: Creatine
fact: Named for kreas, Greek for meat — Chevreul isolated it from a muscle extract in 1832.

name: Citrulline
fact: Named for citrullus, Latin for watermelon — first isolated from the fruit in 1914.

name: Theanine
fact: About 1-2% of green tea leaf by dry weight, discovered there in 1949, isolated in 1950.

name: Caffeine
fact: Runge isolated it from coffee beans Goethe gave him, weeks after they first met, in 1819.

name: Alpha-GPC
fact: Chemically stripped from lecithin — remove its two fatty tails and this is what is left.

name: Synephrine
fact: Citrus makes its own stimulant: tyrosine, then tyramine, then this, in the unripe peel.

name: Horsetail
fact: Absorbs silicon from soil and once scoured pewter — the old name for it is 'pewterwort'.

name: Dandelion
fact: Named for its jagged leaves — French 'dent de lion', lion's tooth.

name: Aloe Vera
fact: Its leaf holds two layers: a water-storing gel, and a laxative called aloin the FDA banned in 2002.

name: Ginseng
fact: Chinese for 'person root' — named for a forked shape said to resemble a human body.

name: Psyllium
fact: About a quarter of the seed's weight is mucilage, milled from its husk into dietary fiber.

name: Fructooligosaccharides
fact: Resists human digestive enzymes; gut bacteria ferment it instead — a genuine dietary fiber.

name: Pineapple
fact: A bromeliad, not a tree. Its flowers fuse into one fruit even without pollination.

name: Spinach
fact: Dioecious and wind-pollinated — separate male and female plants, unusual for a vegetable.

name: Acai
fact: A palm-tree drupe from Amazon floodplains, borne in branched clusters of up to 900 fruit.

name: Pomegranate
fact: Botanically a berry — one flower's ovary, ripened into a fruit holding up to 1,400 seeds.

name: Goji
fact: A woody nightshade shrub — same family as tomato and potato, but no vine in sight.

name: Papaya
fact: Its huge lobed leaves crown a single soft stem up to ten metres tall. No trunk, no wood.

name: Broccoli
fact: Same species as cabbage, bred for the flower head instead of the wrapped leaves.

name: Alfalfa
fact: A legume whose taproot can run past 15 metres, chasing water no shallow root reaches.

name: Biotin
fact: First crystallized from egg yolk in 1936 — but raw egg white's avidin binds it too tightly to absorb.

name: Hyaluronic Acid
fact: A glycosaminoglycan first pulled from a cow's vitreous humor in 1934 — now farmed from rooster combs.

name: Sucralose
fact: E955. Sucrose with three hydroxyls swapped for chlorine — discovered when 'test' was misheard as 'taste.'

name: Stevia
fact: The Guaraní called it ka'a he'ê, sweet herb — its glycosides taste up to 300 times as sweet as sugar.

name: Fish Sauce
fact: Salted and sealed for up to two years — the longer it ferments, the less fishy it tastes.

name: Lithium Graphite
fact: LiC6 — lithium ions parked between graphite's carbon sheets. This is what a battery anode actually is.

name: Lithium Fluoride
fact: The one alkali halide water won't dissolve. Its crystal passes UV light nothing else can.

name: Lithium Chloride
fact: So hungry for water it is used to dry air itself, one damp crystal at a time.

name: Lithium Iodide
fact: The standard electrolyte inside a pacemaker battery — chosen for how long it lasts, not how well it conducts.

name: Lithium Nitride
fact: The only stable alkali metal nitride. Lithium takes nitrogen straight from the air; the others cannot.

name: Sodium Bromide
fact: A sedative for eighty years before anyone knew why — bromide calms nerves whatever salt carries it.

name: Sodium Iodide
fact: Doped with thallium it lights up under radiation — the crystal at the heart of the first particle counters.

name: Potassium Fluoride
fact: After hydrogen fluoride itself, this is chemistry's main working source of a fluoride ion.

name: Caesium Chloride
fact: Spun in a centrifuge it forms its own density gradient — the trick that first separated DNA by weight.

name: Stainless Steel
fact: Steel needs only 10.5% chromium to stop rusting. The chromium grows its own invisible, self-healing skin.

name: Beryllium Copper
fact: Strikes without a spark — the one alloy safe to swing a wrench with beside an open gas line.

name: Niobium-Titanium
fact: Wound into coil and chilled near absolute zero, this is the wire inside four in five MRI magnets.

name: Rose Gold
fact: Gold does not blush on its own. Copper mixed through it is the entire difference.

name: Hard Lead
fact: Pure lead sags. A little antimony stiffens it — and, oddly, stops it shrinking as it cools.

name: Titanium Alloy
fact: Aluminium in the lattice makes titanium fly. This one alloy is most of the titanium ever flown.

name: Iron Chloride
fact: Rust-red and thirsty for grime — it clumps dirt out of drinking water and eats copper off circuit boards.

name: Galvanized Iron
fact: Zinc rusts first on purpose. It sacrifices itself to a scratch so the iron underneath does not have to.

name: Silver Chloride
fact: It darkens the instant light touches it — the whole of photography starts from that one fact.

name: Gold Amalgam
fact: Mercury drinks up gold flour too fine to pan. Miners have used the trick, and paid for it, for centuries.

name: Dental Amalgam
fact: Soft enough to pack into a cavity, hard within minutes: mercury and silver, filling teeth for two centuries.

name: Xenon Tetrafluoride
fact: 1962: proof the noble gases were never entirely noble. The first one ever forced into a bond.

name: Lithium Oxide
fact: A pinch in a glaze turns copper blue and cobalt pink — a flux that changes the colours around it.

name: Sodium Peroxide
fact: Not a simple oxide — sodium burned in excess oxygen overshoots. It once breathed for submarines.

name: Potassium Superoxide
fact: Scrubs carbon dioxide out of sealed air and hands back oxygen — a rebreather's whole trick in one rock.

name: Titanium Dioxide
fact: The white in almost everything white — paint, paper, toothpaste — chosen purely for its brightness.

name: Chromium Oxide
fact: Chrome green, and the reason chromium itself does not rust — a film one molecule thick that heals itself.

name: Nickel Oxide
fact: Green as a pure crystal, black the instant it is not — an electrode inside the earliest nickel batteries.

name: Manganese Dioxide
fact: Half a million tonnes a year go into one job: soaking up electrons inside an ordinary dry-cell battery.

name: Tin Dioxide
fact: Suspended in a glaze it scatters light instead of passing it — the opaque white of old tin-glazed pottery.

name: Palladium Hydride
fact: A palm-sized block of this metal can hold nine hundred times its own volume of hydrogen gas.

name: Neon Light
fact: Thousands of volts through the gas itself, no filament at all. Pure neon burns a steady orange-red.

name: Silver Bromide
fact: More light-sensitive than silver chloride — the compound most black-and-white film was built from.

name: Germanium Dioxide
fact: Mixed into silica glass it bends light more without clouding it — the core of a fiber-optic cable.

name: Bismuth Telluride
fact: Push current through this crystal and one face chills while the other warms — no moving parts.

name: Ferrovanadium
fact: A little of this in the melt is a universal steel hardener — tougher, and better against heat and twisting.

name: NiCd Battery
fact: A cadmium plate and a nickel plate in alkaline electrolyte — rechargeable long before lithium was.

name: Platinum-Rhodium Gauze
fact: Platinum wire mesh with a tenth rhodium worked in — the screen ammonia burns across on its way to fertiliser.

name: Platinum-Iridium
fact: 90% platinum, 10% iridium — for over a century, this exact golf-ball-sized bar WAS the kilogram.

name: Hardened Platinum
fact: Pure platinum is too soft for a ring. A trace of ruthenium worked in is what actually holds the stone.

name: Tungsten-Rhenium
fact: A thermocouple wire good past 2,200°C — hot enough that almost nothing else can even measure it.

name: Rocket Nozzle Alloy
fact: Niobium and hafnium, a whisper of titanium — this exact alloy steered the Apollo Lunar Module down.

name: Scandium-Aluminium Alloy
fact: Traces of scandium in aluminium raise its strength 50 to 70 MPa — enough to matter in a MiG or a bike frame.

name: Yttrium Aluminium Garnet
fact: Yttrium, aluminium and oxygen in a crystal clear enough to host a laser. Dope it with neodymium and it lases.

name: Rubidium Superoxide
fact: Like potassium one row up, rubidium in excess oxygen skips the plain oxide and goes straight to superoxide.

name: Strontium Chloride
fact: The active ingredient behind 'for sensitive teeth' — it plugs the tubules a receding gum has exposed.

name: Luminous Paint
fact: Radium mixed into zinc sulfide, painted onto a watch face, glowing green in the dark since 1908.

name: Gas Mantle
fact: 99% thorium dioxide, 1% cerium dioxide — a fabric mesh that turns an ordinary gas flame white-hot bright.

name: Ferrocerium
fact: Scrape it and the sparks hit 3,300°C. This, not flint, is what actually lights a modern lighter.

name: Neodymium Magnet
fact: Neodymium, iron, and boron this recipe cannot carry — the strongest permanent magnet you can buy.

name: Samarium-Cobalt Magnet
fact: Weaker than neodymium but happy past 300°C — the rare-earth magnet that survives an engine bay.

name: Red Phosphor
fact: Half a gram to a gram of this sits inside every colour tube TV — europium is the only red they had.

name: Gadolinium Steel
fact: As little as 1% gadolinium makes iron easier to work and far harder to oxidise hot.

name: Signal Paint
fact: Promethium's beta rays hit a phosphor instead of your eye directly — a gentler glow than radium's ever was.

name: Nuoc Cham
fact: One part fish sauce, one part sugar, two parts water, lime for the acid — Vietnam's dipping sauce.

name: Carbon Tetrafluoride
fact: Burn carbon in pure fluorine instead of oxygen and this is what comes out — even graphite will burn this way.

name: Carbon Disulfide
fact: For a century this reeking liquid was made by heating carbon and sulfur, before natural gas took the job.

name: Nitrogen Trifluoride
fact: Nitrogen barely reacts with anything — an electric spark through nitrogen and fluorine forces this bond.

name: Chlorine Trifluoride
fact: Made by fluorinating chlorine gas — and so reactive once formed it will set sand itself on fire.

name: Disulfur Dichloride
fact: Lead chlorine gas into a flask of sulfur and the contents turn a golden yellow liquid at room temperature.

name: Phosphorus Trichloride
fact: White phosphorus burning in chlorine gas — the industrial route to one of chemistry's most common reagents.

name: Sulfur Hexafluoride
fact: Discovered in 1901 by simply exposing sulfur to fluorine gas — nothing about making it has changed since.

name: Phosphorus Pentafluoride
fact: Phosphorus and fluorine combine directly, four molecules of each swapped for four of this at a time.

name: Phosphorus Sesquisulfide
fact: Red phosphorus and sulfur, melted together above 450 K — this is the head of a strike-anywhere match.

name: Aluminum Chloride
fact: Aluminium foil burns in chlorine gas at 650°C in an exothermic reaction run at industrial scale.

name: Aluminum Sulfide
fact: Ignite aluminium and sulfur together and the reaction runs so hot the molten product can melt through steel.

name: Copper Chloride
fact: Copper at red heat combines directly with chlorine gas — a very exothermic reaction with a molten result.

name: Magnesium Chloride
fact: Alkaline earth metals all react with the halogens to form salts like this one — magnesium's own chloride.

name: Magnesium Sulfide
fact: Formed directly when sulfur, or even just hydrogen sulfide gas, meets magnesium metal.

name: Calcium Chloride
fact: The textbook example of an alkaline earth metal meeting a halogen — calcium and chlorine, straight to salt.

name: Sodium Sulfide
fact: Sodium and sulfur combine directly, but almost every tonne made goes straight into pulping wood for paper.

name: Potassium Sulfide
fact: Potassium and sulfur react cleanly together, dissolved in liquid ammonia to keep the reaction under control.

name: Tin Chloride
fact: Chlorine gas over tin metal at 115°C, nothing more — a clean, direct route to a common industrial catalyst.

name: Lead Chloride
fact: The most straightforward way to make it is also the most literal: chlorine gas, straight onto lead metal.

name: Gold Chloride
fact: Robert Boyle proved gold could react with something in 1666: metallic gold, straight into chlorine gas.

name: Copper Fluoride
fact: Copper metal and fluorine gas at 500°C — only half of it converts, but the half that does is genuine.

name: Aluminum-Copper Alloy
fact: Aluminium and a little copper, precipitated into a strengthening phase — its main home is an aircraft frame.

name: Magnalium
fact: Aluminium and magnesium alloyed — light enough for engines, or loaded with magnesium for a firework's flare.

name: NaK
fact: Sodium and potassium melted together stay liquid at room temperature — reactor coolant since the 1960s.

name: Tin-Silver Solder
fact: Tin dissolves silver readily — their eutectic, melting at 221°C, is the real alloy behind lead-free solder.

name: Lithium Bromide
fact: A strong aqueous solution of this salt is the desiccant that dries the air inside a building's cooling system.

name: Potassium Bromide
fact: The first medicine that worked against epilepsy — so widely prescribed 'bromide' became slang for dull.

name: Rubidium Fluoride
fact: A white crystal built on the same cubic lattice as ordinary table salt, one row down the periodic table.

name: Rubidium Chloride
fact: Dissolves into cells so readily that biologists use it to make bacteria absorb foreign DNA on command.

name: Rubidium Bromide
fact: Its crystal lattice is table salt's own structure, just stretched to fit two heavier atoms.

name: Rubidium Iodide
fact: Bottled as eye drops in Romania under its own brand name — eight milligrams of this salt in every millilitre.

name: Caesium Fluoride
fact: The most reactive stable metal meets the most reactive nonmetal — chemists use the salt as a fluoride source.

name: Caesium Bromide
fact: Grown into crystal optics, it splits light in spectrophotometers chemists use to identify compounds.

name: Caesium Iodide
fact: The phosphor screen inside an X-ray image intensifier — this crystal is what turns radiation into a picture.

name: Krypton Difluoride
fact: Krypton will not bond with fluorine on its own — only an electric spark, UV light, or a hot wire forces it.

name: Titanium Chloride
fact: Cold titanium ignores chlorine completely. At 550°C the two combine violently instead.

name: Cobalt Chloride
fact: Blue when bone dry, pink the moment it absorbs water — a colour change reliable enough to indicate humidity.

name: Chromium Chloride
fact: Chromium metal chlorinated directly — the same element that grows its own rust-proof skin, made to react.

name: Lanthanum Oxide
fact: Lanthanum tarnishes almost as fast as you can watch, turning black in hours as it burns to this oxide.

name: Cerium Oxide
fact: Ce + O2 → CeO2, straight from the metal — then it scrubs a car exhaust or polishes glass flat.

name: Neodymium Oxide
fact: Burns off the metal at just 150°C, and the flaking oxide keeps exposing fresh metal underneath to burn again.

name: Europium Fluoride
fact: Europium metal reacts with every halogen there is. Fluorine gives this one: white europium(III) fluoride.

name: Europium Chloride
fact: The same europium-plus-halogen reaction, run on chlorine instead — yellow crystals instead of white.

name: Gadolinium Oxide
fact: Unlike most rare earths, gadolinium shrugs off dry air — only damp air tarnishes it down to this oxide.

name: Hydrogen Fluoride
fact: The only common acid that eats glass, not metal — stored in plastic because it dissolves the bottle.

name: Lithium-Ion Battery
fact: Graphite anode, lithium cobalt oxide cathode — the pair that actually powers a phone.

name: Lithium Hydride
fact: 2 Li + H2 → 2 LiH — fast even at low heat, faster still above 600°C.

name: Neptunium
fact: Named for the next planet past Uranus — a neutron fired into uranium made the first atom of it in 1940.

name: Americium
fact: A speck of americium-241 sits inside most household smoke detectors, ionizing air to sense smoke.

name: Curium
fact: Named for Marie and Pierre Curie — first made in 1944 by firing alpha particles at plutonium.

name: Berkelium
fact: Named for Berkeley, California — the same cyclotron there later made californium too.

name: Californium
fact: Half a milligram gives off enough neutrons to start up a nuclear reactor or find oil in a well.

name: Protactinium
fact: Named for the element it decays into — actinium — the step directly before it in nature's decay chains.

name: Actinium
fact: So radioactive it visibly glows pale blue in the dark, one of only a few elements that do.

name: Technetium
fact: The first element ever made artificially before being found in nature — its name literally means 'artificial'.

name: Astatine
fact: So rare that less than a gram of it exists naturally in the entire Earth's crust at any moment.

name: Rutherfordium
fact: Named for Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who first split the atom and mapped out its nucleus.

name: Dubnium
fact: Named for Dubna, Russia — the lab whose decade-long priority dispute with Berkeley became legend.

name: Seaborgium
fact: One of only two elements named for someone still alive at the time — chemist Glenn Seaborg himself.

name: Bohrium
fact: Named for Niels Bohr, who put electrons into orbits around the nucleus like tiny planets.

name: Hassium
fact: Named for Hesse, the German state — Hassia in Latin — home to the lab that first made it in 1984.

name: Meitnerium
fact: The only element named specifically for a real woman — physicist Lise Meitner, co-discoverer of fission.

name: Darmstadtium
fact: Named for Darmstadt, the German city whose heavy-ion accelerator has now made half a dozen elements.

name: Roentgenium
fact: Named for Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays and won physics' very first Nobel Prize.

name: Copernicium
fact: Named for Copernicus, who worked out that the planets circle the Sun rather than the Earth.

name: Beryllium Fluoride
fact: The fluoride base of FLiBe, the molten salt that carries heat through a liquid-fluoride nuclear reactor.

name: Beryllium Chloride
fact: A Friedel-Crafts catalyst, and the raw material electrolysis splits apart to make pure beryllium metal.

name: Beryllium Bromide
fact: Covalent, not ionic — beryllium is too small and too polarizing to make a true salt with a halogen.

name: Beryllium Iodide
fact: Decomposed on a white-hot tungsten filament, it deposits beryllium metal purer than any ore ever gives up.

name: Magnesium Fluoride
fact: Clear from deep ultraviolet to the infrared — the anti-reflective coating on camera and telescope lenses.

name: Magnesium Bromide
fact: Once a nerve tonic and anticonvulsant; today it mostly survives as a catalyst in the aldol reaction.

name: Magnesium Iodide
fact: Made dry, in ether — chemists use it to strip methyl groups clean off an aromatic ether.

name: Calcium Bromide
fact: A dense brine pumped down oil wells as drilling fluid, and stirred into coal to trap mercury before it vents.

name: Calcium Iodide
fact: An iodine supplement stirred into cat food today; an early photographic emulsion a century ago.

name: Strontium Fluoride
fact: Carries radioactive strontium-90 inside a radioisotope thermoelectric generator, decaying for decades.

name: Strontium Bromide
fact: Burned in a flare, it throws off the same deep red any strontium salt gives a firework.

name: Strontium Iodide
fact: Doped with europium it catches gamma rays and flashes — a scintillator crystal grown a whole cylinder at once.

name: Barium Fluoride
fact: Clear to infrared light and flashes at a gamma photon's touch — a crystal PET scanners use as a detector.

name: Barium Chloride
fact: The standard lab reagent for weighing out exactly how much sulfate a solution is hiding.

name: Barium Bromide
fact: Marie Curie used this salt's own crystallization habit to fractionate radium out of its barium ore.

name: Barium Iodide
fact: The least-documented of barium's four halides — even its own reference entry names it no use at all.

name: Radium Fluoride
fact: Crystallizes in fluorite's own cubic shape — the same column of the table, just heavier and radioactive.

name: Radium Chloride
fact: The first radium compound ever isolated pure, by Curie herself — now also a prostate-cancer drug's core.

name: Radium Bromide
fact: Discovered by the Curies in 1898; it later glowed on watch dials until the danger was understood.

name: Radium Iodide
fact: A yellow, water-soluble radium salt — one of the rarest compounds here, one of Wikipedia's shortest pages.

name: Bacteriophage
fact: A virus built to infect nothing but bacteria. The name is Greek for devourer of bacteria — and it means it.

name: Prophage
fact: A phage genome stitched into a bacterium's own chromosome, copied for free at every division. Waiting.

name: Lysis
fact: A cell bursting open once its own internal pressure overcomes a wall that phage enzymes have already breached.

name: Protozoan
fact: A single eukaryotic cell living entirely on its own. Common wherever there's water, even a damp patch of soil.

name: Eimeria
fact: An apicomplexan parasite genus, almost always locked to one host for life. Several live only in chickens.

name: Coccidiosis
fact: An intestinal disease caused by coccidian parasites invading the gut lining. Spread through droppings.

name: Salmonella
fact: A genus of rod-shaped bacteria behind roughly 1.2 million food-poisoning cases a year in the US alone.

name: Viroid
fact: Bare circular RNA, no protein coat, about 1/80th the size of a typical virus. Only known to infect plants.

name: Salicylic Acid
fact: Raffaele Piria split salicin into a sugar and a second piece, then oxidised that piece into this.

name: Aspirin
fact: Felix Hoffmann acetylated salicylic acid in 1897 using acetic anhydride. Bayer called the result aspirin.

name: Streptomyces
fact: Filamentous, spore-forming soil bacteria — as a genus they make over two-thirds of nature's known antibiotics.

name: Streptomycin
fact: Isolated from Streptomyces griseus, 19 October 1943, out of New Jersey soil. The first cure for tuberculosis.

name: Pancreas
fact: Ninety-nine percent of it is exocrine, making digestive enzymes. The other one percent makes insulin.

name: Insulin
fact: Two peptide chains, A and B, held by two disulfide bonds — a third closes a loop inside the A chain.

name: Sweet Potato
fact: A different family from potato entirely. Grown from cuttings of its own vine, not from seed.

name: Cauliflower
fact: Same species as cabbage and broccoli — a head of flower buds that never opened.

name: Zucchini
fact: A squash, picked immature — the seeds and rind are still soft enough to eat.

name: Eggplant
fact: A nightshade, like chilli and tomato — a berry, botanically, that follows the flower.

name: Asparagus
fact: The part eaten is a young shoot — spears sent up each spring by a perennial root.

name: Radish
fact: Ready to pull within a month. Grows best in light, sandy soil for a straight root.

name: Turnip
fact: A biennial root — it spends its first year storing food, and only flowers in its second.

name: Leek
fact: An allium, like onion — grown for up to six months in loose, well-drained soil.

name: Brussels Sprout
fact: A cabbage cultivar bred for its buds, which mature up a thick stalk over several weeks.

name: Kale
fact: A cabbage cultivar whose leaves never form a head — hardy enough to survive -15°C.

name: Artichoke
fact: A cultivated thistle. Its bud must be cut before the flower opens or it turns woody.

name: Okra
fact: A mallow-family seed pod — cotton's cousin — that turns mucilaginous once cut.

name: Mushroom
fact: Agaricus bisporus, the common button mushroom — grown on composted manure, not wood.

name: Avocado
fact: A single-seeded berry. Named varieties are grafted onto rootstock, not grown from seed.

name: Arugula
fact: A mustard-family salad leaf, ready in 40 to 50 days of full sun and moist soil.

name: Rhubarb
fact: The edible part is only the leaf stalk. The leaf blade itself is poisonous — oxalic acid.

name: Watercress
fact: An aquatic mustard relative with hollow floating stems — grows straight in flowing streams.

name: Orange
fact: A citrus hybrid — pomelo crossed with mandarin. Named varieties are grafted, same as lemon's own kin.

name: Grapefruit
fact: An accidental hybrid of sweet orange and pomelo, first crossed in the 17th-century Caribbean.

name: Peach
fact: A stone fruit that starts bearing within 2-3 years — and is finished within about 20.

name: Plum
fact: A stone fruit of Prunus, kept pruned to a modest 5-6 metres for picking.

name: Apricot
fact: A stone fruit. The kernel inside the pit is not a snack — it carries a real cyanide compound.

name: Nectarine
fact: Not a hybrid — the same species as peach, missing fuzz because of one recessive gene.

name: Watermelon
fact: 91% water. Botanically a pepo — a modified berry with a thick rind.

name: Cantaloupe
fact: Cucumis melo — a true melon, the same genus as cucumber, not related to watermelon.

name: Kiwi
fact: A berry from a woody vine — and the vine itself is either male or female, never both.

name: Raspberry
fact: An aggregate of tiny drupelets. Its cane grows one year and only fruits the next.

name: Blackberry
fact: Same aggregate-drupelet fruit as raspberry, but the core stays in when you pick it.

name: Cranberry
fact: Harvested by flooding the bed — the ripe berries float free of the vine.

name: Blueberry
fact: A true berry that changes colour three times before it's ripe — green, then red, then blue.

name: Date
fact: A palm's drupe. Wild-pollinated by wind — growers do it by hand for a reliable crop.

name: Persimmon
fact: Ripens after its own tree has already dropped its leaves for the year.

name: Guava
fact: A myrtle-family tree berry — fruiting within two years of its own seed, for up to forty.

name: Rye
fact: A wheat-tribe cereal that survives snow cover heavy enough to kill winter wheat.

name: Quinoa
fact: Not a grain at all — a seed, from a plant related to spinach, not to wheat.

name: Buckwheat
fact: No relation to wheat — it's a cousin of rhubarb, eaten like a grain only because of its starch.

name: Millet
fact: Small-seeded, drought-tolerant grasses grown as a grain across dry regions worldwide.

name: Sorghum
fact: A grass grain bred for drought and heat — nitrogen-efficient where most cereals struggle.

name: Chickpea
fact: A pulse — each small pod on the plant holds only two or three seeds.

name: Bean
fact: Phaseolus vulgaris — black, kidney and pinto beans are all one species, bred different colours.

name: Black Bean
fact: The common bean, dried — anthocyanin pigment in the seed coat is what turns it black.

name: Pinto Bean
fact: Spanish for 'painted' — named for the mottled speckling on its seed coat.

name: Kidney Bean
fact: A common bean cultivar. Raw, it carries the highest lectin toxin load of any bean.

name: Semolina
fact: A coarser grind than flour — the granules couscous and pasta both start from.

name: Couscous
fact: Semolina rolled wet by hand into tiny pellets, then steamed light and fluffy.

name: Cinnamon
fact: Inner tree bark, pried off in strips that curl into quills as they dry.

name: Nutmeg
fact: A seed, sun-dried for up to 30 weeks until it rattles loose in its own shell.

name: Clove
fact: Not a seed or a berry — a flower bud, picked before it ever opens.

name: Cardamom
fact: Ginger's own family — triangular papery pods holding small black seeds.

name: Vanilla
fact: An orchid's seed pod. Every plant grown today is hand-pollinated — its own flower can't self-pollinate.

name: Saffron
fact: The dried stigma of an autumn crocus. A kilogram takes 150,000 flowers, hand-picked.

name: Fennel
fact: Carrot's own family — its dried seeds are the spice, its bulb the vegetable.

name: Mustard Seed
fact: Cabbage's own family — the small round seed the whole mustard condiment starts from.

name: Allspice
fact: Picked green and unripe, then sun-dried until it looks like a large peppercorn.

name: Star Anise
fact: A star-shaped fruit of 6 to 8 pods in a whorl, picked from the tree just before it ripens.

name: Wasabi
fact: A real Brassicaceae rhizome, ground fresh — most 'wasabi' served is horseradish and dye.

name: Cashew
fact: A drupe hanging off the cashew apple. Its shell carries a poison-ivy relative — toxic until roasted.

name: Pistachio
fact: A drupe whose shell pops open on its own as it ripens — a trait people bred for.

name: Pecan
fact: Not really a nut — a hickory drupe, a single stone inside a husk.

name: Hazelnut
fact: A true nut, unlike most 'nuts' here — it drops free of its husk 7 to 8 months after pollination.

name: Macadamia
fact: A Proteaceae tree native to Australia. Perfectly edible for people — toxic to dogs.

name: Mozzarella
fact: Pasta filata — curd heated and kneaded until it turns into one smooth, stretchy paste.

name: Cheddar
fact: Named for the process, not the place — curd repeatedly kneaded, cut, stacked and turned to drain the whey.

name: Parmesan
fact: Hard and granular from unpasteurised cow's milk, aged a minimum of a year and often two.

name: Feta
fact: Greek and brined — sheep's milk, or a mix of sheep and goat, never cow alone.

name: Cottage Cheese
fact: Acid-set curds, drained and mixed straight back with cream — never aged, never pressed.

name: Evaporated Milk
fact: Milk with 60% of its water boiled off, canned and heat-sterilised — no sugar added.

name: Condensed Milk
fact: Evaporated milk with sugar stirred in at a roughly 9:11 ratio — the sugar is what keeps it shelf-stable.

name: Custard
fact: Cream thickened by egg protein alone — coagulating between 70 and 80°C, curdling past it.

name: Ketchup
fact: Tomato, sugar and vinegar — the vinegar and sugar are what keep it shelf-stable.

name: Maple Syrup
fact: Boiled down from tree sap — it takes 20 to 50 litres of sap for one litre of syrup.

name: Peanut Butter
fact: Roasted peanuts, ground twice — medium, then fine — until it's a paste.

name: Jam
fact: Crushed fruit and sugar, boiled to 104°C — the fruit's own pectin is what sets it.

name: Cornstarch
fact: Pure starch, milled out of the corn kernel's endosperm — nothing else left in it.

name: Baking Soda
fact: NaHCO3 — releases carbon dioxide the moment it meets acid or heat, which is the entire trick.

name: Baking Powder
fact: Baking soda pre-mixed with a weak acid and cornstarch — self-contained, unlike soda alone.

name: Worcestershire Sauce
fact: A fermented anchovy-and-malt-vinegar sauce, invented by two Worcester pharmacists.

name: Hot Sauce
fact: Chilli and vinegar, at its simplest — nothing more is required.

name: Tahini
fact: Ground sesame seeds, toasted first — an oily paste, not unlike peanut butter's own process.

name: Vanilla Extract
fact: Vanilla pods steeped in ethanol and water — carries hundreds of flavour compounds beyond vanillin alone.

name: Mustard
fact: Ground mustard seed mixed with vinegar or another liquid into a paste.

name: Shrimp
fact: A decapod crustacean built for swimming — an elongated body, not a crab's sideways scuttle.

name: Crab
fact: Its tail is folded flat under its own body — that's the trait that lets it run sideways.

name: Lobster
fact: Ten legs by the strict count — the two big front pincers are legs too.

name: Salmon
fact: Born in a river, grown at sea, and it fights back upstream to the exact place it hatched.

name: Tuna
fact: A fish that runs warmer than the water around it — one of only three that can.

name: Guacamole
fact: Mashed avocado and salt, traditionally worked with a mortar and pestle.

name: Hummus
fact: Cooked mashed chickpeas blended with tahini — the two ingredients that make it hummus.

name: Salsa
fact: Chopped tomato and onion at its simplest — the base every other salsa builds from.

name: Coleslaw
fact: Shredded raw cabbage in a dressing — cabbage is the only ingredient every recipe agrees on.

name: Omelette
fact: Beaten egg, fried in butter — the whole dish is just that one transformation.

name: Pancake
fact: A starch batter, cooked flat on a hot griddle — no patterned plates involved.

name: Waffle
fact: Leavened batter, cooked between two patterned plates — the grid is pressed in, not poured.

name: Burger
fact: Ground meat, cooked into a patty, inside a sliced bun — the whole definition in one line.

name: Hot Dog
fact: A cooked sausage in a partially sliced bun — nothing more is required to call it one.

name: Sandwich
fact: Any filling between two slices of bread — the bread is the only fixed part of the definition.

name: Fried Rice
fact: Cooked rice, stir-fried — the day-old rice recipe every household reaches for.

name: Taco
fact: A tortilla folded by hand around a filling and eaten straight from the hand.

name: Cassava
fact: Unlike a potato's swollen stem, cassava's edible part really is a root — swollen with starch, and, raw, laced with cyanogenic compounds that processing has to remove.

name: Tapioca
fact: Cassava root, grated and pressed until its starch washes out as a milky liquid, then dried into flour or pearls — raw cassava is toxic, so this processing is not optional.

name: Avibirnavirus
fact: A double-stranded RNA genus, bare and non-enveloped. Its only member's natural hosts are chickens and turkeys.

name: Gumboro Disease
fact: Also called infectious bursal disease. Destroys a young chicken's B-lymphocytes right where they form.

name: Gammacoronavirus
fact: A coronavirus genus from the avian gene pool. Goose, duck and chicken each carry their own species in it.

name: Infectious Bronchitis
fact: A chicken-only coronavirus disease. Fouls the airway first, then can reach the kidney and the oviduct.

name: E. coli
fact: Normal gut flora in almost every warm-blooded animal, harmless there — until one strain gets the wrong genes.

name: Colibacillosis
fact: What a virulent E. coli strain causes once it reaches tissue the harmless kind never goes. Costly to poultry.

name: Ascaridia galli
fact: A roundworm living nowhere but a bird's small intestine. Free-range chickens catch it from an earthworm.

name: Ascaridiasis
fact: Heavy Ascaridia galli infection in a chicken's gut, from eggs that persist for years in soil and water.

name: Satellite
fact: Bare RNA even smaller than a viroid's. It cannot replicate at all without borrowing a helper virus's proteins.

name: Cowpox
fact: A real Orthopoxvirus — its usual wild host is voles, not cattle, which only catch it occasionally.

name: Vaccine
fact: A weakened, killed, or fragmentary pathogen, given on purpose so the immune system meets the real one first.

name: Immunity
fact: The immune system's memory of a pathogen it has already met — faster and stronger, the second time around.

name: Nitrophenol
fact: Phenol with a nitro group on its fourth carbon. Bright yellow, and paracetamol's classical first step.

name: Aminophenol
fact: Nitrophenol's nitro group, reduced to an amine. One reaction away from paracetamol.

name: Paracetamol
fact: Relieves pain and fever. Exactly how is still not settled science, after more than a century of use.

name: Histamine
fact: One amino acid, one step. The actual cause of a runny nose in an allergic reaction — not the allergen protein.

name: Arachidonic Acid
fact: A polyunsaturated fatty acid built into cell-membrane phospholipids until an enzyme cuts it free.

name: Prostaglandin
fact: Made from arachidonic acid by the enzyme painkillers target. The real signal behind pain, fever and swelling.

name: Beryllium Oxide
fact: 2 Be + O2 → 2 BeO — though igniting beryllium in open air also throws off the nitride Be3N2 alongside it.

name: Strontium Oxide
fact: Strontia — what strontium becomes the moment it meets oxygen.

name: Barium Oxide
fact: 2 Ba + O2 → 2 BaO — barium's own exothermic answer to open air.

name: Caesium Superoxide
fact: When caesium burns in air, CsO2 — not the plain oxide — is what actually forms.

name: Calcium Hydride
fact: Calcium and hydrogen, combined directly at 300 to 400°C.

name: Magnesium Hydride
fact: Magnesium, hydrogenated directly — though the first prep needed 200 atmospheres and 500°C.

name: Strontium Hydride
fact: Sr + H2 → SrH2 — a clean yield takes oxygen-free hydrogen and redistilled strontium.

name: Barium Hydride
fact: Barium and hydrogen, combined directly at 150 to 200°C.

name: Sodium Hydride
fact: 2 Na + H2 → 2 NaH — industrially, molten sodium beaten into mineral oil under a hydrogen atmosphere.

name: Potassium Hydride
fact: Potassium and hydrogen, combined directly between 200 and 350°C.

name: Rubidium Hydride
fact: Rubidium metal, treated with hydrogen gas.

name: Caesium Hydride
fact: Made from caesium carbonate and magnesium, heated together in hydrogen.

name: Beryllium Nitride
fact: Beryllium powder, heated in dry nitrogen with oxygen kept well out of the way.

name: Calcium Nitride
fact: 3 Ca + N2 → Ca3N2, straight from the elements.

name: Strontium Nitride
fact: What's left when strontium metal burns in nitrogen instead of air.

name: Barium Nitride
fact: Barium, like the rest of its column, reacts with nitrogen on heating.

name: Radium Nitride
fact: The reason a piece of radium goes black in air: not oxide, nitride. 3 Ra + N2 → Ra3N2.

name: Bromine Trifluoride
fact: Br2 + 3 F2 → 2 BrF3, first made in 1906 by reacting the two straight at 20°C.

name: Iodine Pentafluoride
fact: I2 + 5 F2 → 2 IF5 — first made in 1891 by burning solid iodine in fluorine gas, and still the method today.

name: Bromine Monochloride
fact: One part bromine, one part chlorine, forced together — an interhalogen like any other in its family.

name: Iodine Monochloride
fact: I2 + Cl2 → 2 ICl — chlorine gas passed straight through iodine crystals leaves a dark brown liquid behind.

name: Iodine Monobromide
fact: I2 + Br2 → 2 IBr — the two heaviest common halogens, combined directly.

name: Hydrogen Bromide
fact: Hydrogen and bromine, combined between 200 and 400°C, usually over a platinum catalyst.

name: Hydrogen Iodide
fact: H2 + I2 → 2 HI — the reaction still used to make the highest-purity samples today.

name: Bull
fact: Fertile from about seven months old. Only a few are kept intact — most male calves are castrated.

name: Heifer
fact: A female that has not yet calved. Dairy heifers are often kept on to replace their own mothers.

name: Steer
fact: A castrated male raised for beef. The same animal, elsewhere, might just as easily be called an ox.

name: Chick
fact: Uses an egg tooth to break out of the shell after about 21 days, feeding at first on its last yolk.

name: Cockerel
fact: A young male chicken — not yet the rooster he will grow into.

name: Pullet
fact: A young female chicken, sexually immature — under about 22 weeks old in the poultry trade.

name: Rooster
fact: A fertile adult male chicken. The word is an 18th-century American euphemism for 'cock'.

name: Hen
fact: An adult female chicken. One bred for laying can produce more than 300 eggs a year.

name: Capon
fact: A male chicken castrated or neutered young, traditionally to make the meat milder and fattier.

name: Ram
fact: An intact male sheep, occasionally called a tup. Kept mostly for breeding.

name: Ewe
fact: An adult female sheep. Pronounced 'yoo' — nothing like it looks spelled.

name: Wether
fact: A castrated male sheep. Most male lambs not kept for breeding become one.

name: Kid
fact: A juvenile goat. The word comes from Old Norse kið, carried in by Scandinavian settlers.

name: Buck
fact: An intact adult male goat. Acquires a strong, distinctive odour during the autumn rut.

name: Doe
fact: An adult female goat. Many breeders wait until she reaches 70% of adult weight before breeding.

name: Piglet
fact: Newborn into a litter that was once yearly — by the 19th century, twice a year in Europe.

name: Boar
fact: A male pig of breeding age, kept intact rather than castrated.

name: Gilt
fact: A young female pig, not yet mated or not yet farrowed — the exact line shifts by local usage.

name: Barrow
fact: A male pig castrated before puberty — a stag is the same operation done after.

name: Sow
fact: A breeding female pig, or one after her first or second litter.

name: Foal
fact: An equine up to one year old. A mare 'in foal' is pregnant; to 'foal' is to give birth.

name: Colt
fact: A male foal — the term holds until the horse turns three or four.

name: Filly
fact: A female foal — the term holds until the horse turns three or four.

name: Stallion
fact: An intact adult male horse — a colt becomes one at three, or four in racing.

name: Mare
fact: An adult female horse — a filly becomes one at three, or four in racing.

name: Gelding
fact: A castrated male horse, of any age — the one horse term untouched by puberty.

name: Water Buffalo
fact: Swamp-type buffaloes wallow on purpose, digging mudholes with their own horns.

name: Carabeef
fact: Buffalo meat — the word is a 1970s Philippine-English portmanteau of carabao and beef.

name: Chevon
fact: Goat meat. A 1922 trade-association coinage — chevre crossed with mouton — that never caught on.

name: Donkey
fact: Descended from the African wild ass, at home in true desert rather than open grassland.

name: Rabbit
fact: Livestock since at least the first century BC in Rome, kept for meat, fur and wool.

name: Drake
fact: An adult male duck — 'duck' itself technically names the female, or 'hen' in ornithology.

name: Duckling
fact: A young duck in downy plumage. In the food trade the word can also mean a tender young adult.

name: Goose
fact: Paired with 'gander' it means specifically the female; alone it can mean either sex.

name: Gander
fact: An adult male goose. Set beside 'goose' it draws a sex line the word alone does not.

name: Gosling
fact: A young goose before fledging — not yet able to fly.

name: Poult
fact: An infant turkey — 'chick' works too, but poult is the word specific to it.

name: Tom Turkey
fact: An adult male turkey, also called a gobbler — up to twice the weight of the hen.

name: Turkey Hen
fact: An adult female turkey, typically 2.5 to 5.4 kg — much smaller than the tom.
